articles.title: UNGA: World leaders discuss AI, global conflicts
articles.body:
UNGA: World leaders discuss AI, global conflicts
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 23, 2026
What you need to know
- Artificial intelligence, the Iran war, and climate change set to dominate debate on second day of UN General Assembly
- Trump was among the first speakers to take the stage and said he had a "big decision" to make on Iran, to either make a deal or "annihilate" the country
- Gathering of world leaders takes place against a backdrop of global conflicts, environmental crisis and massive technical disruption
Read below for all the top headlines, videos and analyses on the 81 UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Brazil, Germany, India and Japan renew calls for Security Council reform
The foreign ministers of Brazil, Germany, India and Japan on Wednesday called for the reform of the UN Security Council (UNSC), saying it was more urgent than ever.
"Given the increasingly challenging geopolitical environment, UNSC reform is more necessary than ever before," the four foreign ministers said in a joint statement issued after the diplomats met on Tuesday.
The Security Council is a 15-member body with five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the UK and US — known as the P5 and 10 rotating members elected to two-year terms by the General Assembly.
Permanent members enjoy veto powers, which often means the body is kept from carrying out resolutions due to conflicts with the interests of one or more of them.
UNGA day 2: AI, Iran war, climate to dominate debate
Beyond speeches by the presidents of Syria, Iran and Ukraine, artificial intelligence (AI), the US-Israeli war in Iran and the still-pressing issue of climate change are set to dominate the agenda at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Wednesday.
On day 2 of this 81st UNGA session, tech industry leaders Sam Altman (OpenAI), Dario Amodei (Anthropic) and Clement Delangue (Hugging Face) will brief an emergency meeting of the 15-member UN Security Council. Their attendance comes as international concerns — raised from within the industry — prompt debate over slowing AI development before the new technology potentially spins out of control with unknown consequences.
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday blasted calls to slow the technology as part of a "globalist scheme," brushing aside warnings that it could wipe out humanity within years if left unchecked.
After Trump used his General Assembly speech on Tuesday to threaten the annihilation of Iran and to drive its people "into hell," the Islamic Republic's President Masoud Pezeshkian will directly address world leaders for the first time since the start of the war against Iran in February.
The conflict in Iran has settled into a hot stalemate, directly impacting neighboring states militarily and the entire globe economically.
Iranian and US representatives have met on the sidelines of the General Assembly in New York, but, as has been the case for months, a peace deal remains elusive and the flow of oil through the blockaded Strait of Hormuz stunted.
Russia's more than four-and-a-half-year full-scale assault on Ukraine will also be the topic of diplomatic debate on Wednesday, with a Security Council session scheduled for the morning and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy set to address the General Assembly in the afternoon.
Lastly, climate urgency is on the slate, with outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blasting fossil fuel giants for treating the Earth's atmosphere like an "open sewer" for emissions.
He further chided "big oil" for its greed as the world grapples with armed conflict.
"Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, five major Western oil companies have pocketed nearly half a trillion dollars in profits," he said, noting that at the same time just $34 billion (€29.8 billion) had been invested in helping developing countries adapt to a warming world.
Thanks for reading — we'll be back with more soon
Thanks for following this blog for on the first day of the UN General Assembly debate. We'll restart coverage later on Wednesday for day 2 of the event.
What's expected on Wednesday?
On day 2 of the debate, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to take the stage as his country fends off Russia for another winter. US top diplomat Marco Rubio is also expected to meet his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines on Wednesday.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is slated to speak Wednesday, as the US continues its war with Iran.
The UN Security Council will also hold a meeting on AI. Open AI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei are expected to attend the session.
US top diplomat Rubio to meet Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov on Wednesday
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will meet Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York City on Wednesday morning, the US State Department said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with President Donald Trump at the UN headquarters on Tuesday to discuss an end to the 4-year-old war with Russia, including a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets.
UK's Andy Burnham: 'Britain is back'
In his debut as UK prime minister at the UNGA debate, Andy Burnham declared "Britain is back" 10 years after the country dealt with the turbulence caused by Brexit.
Burnham said the UK is "restoring our stability" and "building a more dynamic economy" while seeking trade and working together with other countries to tackle shared problems.
However, he said the UK needs to deal with forces of division and instability. He said this begins with Britain boosting its defense expenditures as a NATO member state and strengthening European capabilities.
Another issue Burnham addressed was disinformation being sowed online by Russia-aligned actors.
"Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fear," Burnham said. "They've used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles. Forged the branding of 28 British organizations — including universities and the BBC. They've amplified far-right narratives."
The UK prime minister said there is evidence that Russia tried to interfere in the 2019 UK general election. He said the Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion ($1.7 billion, €1.5 billion) annually to sow disinformation.
As a solution, Burnham announced the National Centre for Information Defence to fight disinformation which hurts British interests.
Burnham also addressed the issue of AI, saying global standards are needed because "fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance." Burnham said the UK will work on convincing other countries regarding rules on AI transparency and access to AI models.
Japan's mission is to lead efforts towards world without nuclear weapons, Takaichi says
Japan's conservative Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said it her country's "mission" to lead efforts towards a "world without nuclear weapons."
She said this is because Japan is the "the only country to have ever suffered atomic bombings during war." The US atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki during World War II in 1945 killed and maimed hundreds of thousands people, with the radiation causing illnesses in survivors in the years after.
Takaichi urged a stronger Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty regime. She also warned that North Korea's nuclear and missile programs along with other activities are a "serious threat to international peace and security."
In regards to technology, Takaichi said Japan intends to host an AI safety summit in the future.
The Japanese prime minister also called for a reform of the UN Security Council by expanding both the number of permanent and non-permanent members.
IN PICTURES: Mongolia, Vietnam, Dominica among afternoon speakers
Here are some photos of leaders who spoke during this afternoon's session of the UNGA:
North Korea's vice foreign minister traveling to UNGA
North Korea's Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs Kim Son Gyong has departed from Pyongyang to attend the UN General Assembly debate in New York City, North Korean state media outlet KCNA reported.
It's unclear whether Kim will meet with officials from the Trump administration.
During his first term, Trump pushed for a deal where North Korea would give up its nuclear ambitions in exchange for sanctions relief.
Trump had met with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Singapore, Hanoi and the Korean Demilitarized Zone in 2018 and 2019 to discuss a possible deal, but ultimately a final agreement never materialized after talks broke down in Sweden in October 2019.
Zelenskyy meets Trump, says US and Ukraine want war to end before winter
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly debate.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy characterized the meeting with Trump as "positive and productive."
"Both the US and Ukraine want to see this senseless Russian war ended before winter. We discussed potential de-escalatory steps that can open up the way to diplomacy," Zelenskyy said.
"I am grateful that in the meantime our teams keep working on launching Patriot interceptor production in Ukraine. This is what will help proect lives, should Russia spurn the negotiations and keep betting on ballistic missile terror against our people this winter and beyond," the Ukrainian leader added.
Zelenskyy said he also discussed a winter package of air defense for Ukraine with Trump, among other issues.
The negotiation process between Ukraine and Russia is still stalled, with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner visiting Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month to jumpstart the talks. It comes as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine will hit its 5-year anniversary in February 2027.
In comments to journalists after the 40-minute meeting, Zelenskyy said the two leaders discussed an energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy said "we are ready for any kind of format of energy ceasefire" if Russia agrees to "not attack our energy system."
Trump has criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. He has, without evidence, blamed the Ukrainian attacks for raising the price of diesel fuel, as the US war with Iran disrupts energy shipments from the Strait of Hormuz.
Macron calls for open-source AI model not dependent on US, China
Towards the end of his wide-ranging address, French President Emmanuel Macron said there was a need for nations to develop their own artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities so as not to be beholden to the US and China.
"France is proud to have a competitive frontier model" he said, likely referring to Mistral AI.
Macron said likeminded nations such as India, Brazil, Singapore, African nations and the Gulf states should pool not only their financial resources but also their data processing capacity.
"I don't want anyone to become the vassal of one of the great powers. Rather, we must come together to build an open-source frontier model, a cutting-edge model," he told the UN General Assembly.
"Our investment capabilities must be pooled to build a cutting-edge open-source AI model, which we will share. We should not depend on somebody else," he added.
Macron: 'Shame on all of us' of failing to do more for Gaza
French President Emmanuel Macron was addressing the General Assembly for the last time, as his term limit approaches and presidential elections beckon early next year.
He alluded to his previous visit to the event in New York, when a dozen countries including France announced plans to recognize Palestinian statehood.
"I understand that some of you are very cynical," Macron said, and some people would argue this recognition was only on paper and did not address the reality of the situation.
"But what is our credibility worth if we remain inactive on Gaza?" he asked. "Some claim that peace has been achieved, but this has not opened up humanitarian deliveries. The scenes, the spectacle, it is shameful. Shame on all of us!"
Macron said that what was needed was respect for the "legitimate rights" of the Palestinian people, arguing that this was a "prerequisite for security" not just for Palestinians but also for Israel.
"But all those who claim that Israel's security requires the violation of the sovereignty of all of its neighboring states are making a very fateful error," Macron said. "They are weakening Israel's security, today, and going forward. They are threatening Israel's security, in fact."
What did Macron suggest regarding Ukraine?
Macron said that France and its allies would continue providing "unstinting support" to Kyiv, but he also floated a suggestion similar to those made by others involved either in the conflict or the efforts to broker a stop to the fighting.
He proposed a "double moratorium," saying that both Ukraine and Russia should commit to stop strikes on each others's energy infrastructure and on grain shipments in the Black Sea.
"Winter is coming," Macron said, explaining, "We'd like to express our support [for] a double moratorium. A moratorium on strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure, that's first. And a Black Sea moratorium which would allow us to release grain shipments."
In times of peace both Russia and Ukraine are prolific agricultural exporters, and use the Black Sea to ship their produce.
Part of supporting Ukraine, Macron said, was working to ensure that "useful negotiations" between the two sides start as quickly as possible. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was attending Tuesday's session; Russia's Vladimir Putin was not expected to travel to New York, or at least he has not done so since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Trump tells reporters US and Iranian officials met
A few hours after his speech at the assembly warning he was prepared to "annihilate" Iran if necessary, US President Donald Trump told reporters that American and Iranian officials had met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
"The had a very good meeting, a very productive meeting," Trump told reporters, saying it had lasted roughly three hours.
"They have another one scheduled in the very near future," he said.
Trump's speech, not unusually for the US president, contained mixed messages on Iran: a combination both of bombastic threats but also assertions that a "deal" to end the fighting was also a realistic prospect.
"I have a big decision to make,” Trump had said during his speech earlier. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
Finland's Stubb: Choose cooperation, and competition, over conflict
Finland's President Alexander Stubb told the audience that the world faced a "choice between cooperation and conflict."
He said that a third "c" was natural and should not cause concern, provided the right balance was struck.
"Competition will always be there. Nations compete now harder than they did a generation ago. This doesn't worry me. What does, is that more and more of them now compete against the rules on which the international order rests," Stubb said.
Stubb said he wanted to defend those rules and the spirit of cooperation and multilateralism underpinning them.
"Small nations need it to survive, and large nations need it to be great," said Stubb, president of a country with a population only around the size of the US state of South Carolina or the Chinese city of Jinan.
Stubb said the rules were the best ways to ensure "that competition does not escalate into conflict, and that cooperation gains ground."
Stubb cited a quote, that itself seemed a riff on another Winston Churchill adage, that's sometimes attributed to former US Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott: "Multilateralism is hell and can be a real pain in the neck, but it is the best option for humanity as a whole."
The Finnish president said that "currently, however, we appear to be going the other way — more towards a non-cooperative and multi-polar world order."
Though he said he see it might be tempting, particularly for larger powers, he called it a fundamentally "short-sighted approach" that "will turn against us, whether you represent a great power, a middle power, or a small state like Finland."
Lithuania's President Nauseda urges assembly not to forget Ukraine
The first Baltic leader to speak, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda, began by delineating his country's plans to help defusing mines in the Strait of Hormuz or helping bring about the Gaza peace plan — but he urged the assembly not to forget the longer-running conflict closest to his home.
"Ladies and gentleman, the one conflict that poses the greatest threat to the world order is Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine," Nauseda said, even 12 years after it began with the annexation of Crimea and the beginnings of a Russian-backed uprising in eastern Ukraine.
In that time, Nauseda said, "Russia has escalated from clandestine operations and limited warfare in eastern Ukraine to massive military operations, mass killings, and ultimately the largest drone attacks against civilian infrastructure the world has ever seen."
He noted how the full-blown war, starting with Russia's February 2022 invasion, had now lasted longer than the first World War. Nauseda said that despite massive casualties, Russian progress had slowed to a snail's pace and Ukraine's culture, language and institutions stood tall.
Nauseda said that only a Ukrainian victory could safeguard ideals like the UN Charter.
"What we cannot allow is brute force prevailing over international law," he said. "We cannot tolerate any longer Moscow's colonial aspirations."
He said these aspirations reached far into "Europe, Africa and Asia," and said that no country should consider itself immune.
In Lithuania's case, he said Russia's war of aggression had led to "numerous violations of our airspace by combat drones," to intensified hybrid attacks, disinformation and sabotage efforts.
He said that where Russia advanced in opening this "new Pandora's box of new techniques for destablization, other hostile actors follow, learning new skills and ideas."
Qatar's emir says Gulf going through 'one of its most dangerous phases'
Qatar's Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said the current crisis in the Gulf "should come as no surprise to anyone" as he took to the podium in New York.
"It is the cumulative result of years of postponing crisis management through temporary solutions and unrealistic policies," he said of the war between the US and Iran which has sprawled to impact a series of Gulf states.
"At the heart of the dangerous situation we are witnessing lies an absence of a regional system of collective security," Al Thani said. "One that respects the sovereignty, security and territorial integrity of states. One that promotes the peaceful settlement of disputes and the non-interference in the internal affairs of states."
He said Qatar had recently called "from this very podium" for such a system and was now reiterating the appeal "after recent events have demonstrated the urgent need for it."
The emir said, without naming Iran or the US at any point in his address, that the absence of such a regional accord had allowed "one party to drag its neighbors into a war that is not theirs, targeting their vital assets and installations, despite their strenuous efforts to avert escalation."
Iran has sometimes struck targets in neighboring Gulf countries with close ties to the US.
Al Thani said that the restrictions on passage through the Strait of Hormuz amounted to the "lifelines of the global economy" being turned into bargaining chips, "with people on every continent bearing the cost, despite being far removed from the causes of the conflict."
The 46-year-old head of state said this was driving up prices not just for fuel but also for core other goods like food and medicine.

articles.title: From Shaheds to missiles: How Russia is reshaping Iran's arsenal
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
From Shaheds to supersonic missiles: How Russia is reshaping Iran's arsenal
Russia has reportedly been helping Iran to develop an advanced supersonic cruise missile capability, offering Tehran something potentially more consequential than another weapons delivery: the technical knowledge needed to develop the system at home.
According to a Financial Times investigation based on leaked Russian correspondence, travel records, and military patents, the covert programme, codenamed C430L, began in 2023 and has continued during the current US-Israeli war with Iran.
The programme has brought senior specialists from Russian missile manufacturer NPO Mashinostroyenia into direct contact with Iran's defence establishment. Their work has focused on helping Tehran develop ramjet propulsion, which allows cruise missiles to sustain supersonic speeds while flying through the atmosphere.
Iran has already built and flight-tested a ramjet propulsion system, although there is currently no evidence that a Russian-assisted missile has entered operational service.
Russian engineers reportedly analysed Iranian flight-test data and advised their counterparts on technical problems involving fuel systems, combustion stability, air intakes and engine nozzles.
The distinction matters. Rather than selling Tehran a finished Russian missile, Moscow appears to be helping Iranian engineers overcome technological barriers that have constrained their own programme for years.
If successful, that assistance could eventually allow Iran to manufacture and further develop a new family of advanced cruise missiles independently.
Closing a gap in Iran's arsenal
Iran already possesses the Middle East's largest and most diverse missile arsenal, including ballistic missiles, land-attack cruise missiles, and increasingly sophisticated anti-ship weapons.
Yet sustained supersonic cruise flight has remained a significant technological challenge. Tehran has pursued the capability for years. Iranian officials announced plans for supersonic anti-ship missiles in 2016, while two Iranian diplomats were arrested in Ukraine in 2018 while allegedly attempting to obtain components and documentation relating to the Soviet-designed Kh-31A anti-ship missile.
The military value would be particularly significant at sea. “A supersonic anti-ship cruise missile can fill an important gap in Iran's naval arsenal,” Farzin Nadimi, Senior Fellow at the Washington Institute, told The New Arab.
Unlike ballistic missiles descending from higher trajectories, a ramjet-powered cruise missile could approach a vessel at low altitude while travelling at Mach 2 or Mach 3, reducing detection and interception time. Iran’s anti-ship ballistic missiles have so far failed to strike manoeuvring US carriers or destroyers during the current conflict, while, according to Nadimi, a sea-skimming supersonic weapon would leave Aegis-equipped vessels considerably less time to respond.
“That is the threat to the Gulf of Oman/Arabian Sea picket that now holds the blockade,” he said.
The threat could extend further offshore if an air-launched variant were eventually integrated with more modern combat aircraft. Iran has been seeking Russian fighters for years as part of an effort to modernise an air force still largely reliant on aircraft acquired before the 1979 revolution. Leaked Russian documents indicate that a contract covering military aircraft for Iran was signed as early as June 2021 and continued to be implemented after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The first tangible result was the delivery of Yak-130 advanced jet trainers to Iran in 2023. At least eight are reported to have reached the country, providing Tehran with a modern platform for advanced pilot training and a potential bridge towards operating more capable Russian fighters.
The Su-35 would represent the much more significant step. Reports in July suggested that Russia had completed the first 20 fighters destined for Iran, part of what leaked documents have indicated could eventually become a considerably larger fleet, although deliveries and their eventual operational status remain uncertain.
Nadimi argues that pairing a supersonic anti-ship missile with such an aircraft could move the launch point away from Iran’s Makran coast and increase the risks facing US naval forces operating deeper in the Arabian Sea.
For the moment, however, the missile capability itself appears to remain developmental. Hamidreza Azizi, Senior Iran Analyst at the International Crisis Group, pointed to Iran’s recent unsuccessful missile attacks against US naval forces as evidence that Russian assistance “has probably not yet reached an operational level”.
From Iranian drones to Russian know-how
C430L nevertheless reveals how much the military relationship between Moscow and Tehran has changed since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Iran initially emerged as the supplier. From 2022, Tehran provided Russia with Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 one-way attack drones and subsequently helped Moscow establish domestic production, alongside transfers of short-range ballistic missiles.
Russia then adapted Iranian technology to its own battlefield requirements. Russian-produced Geran variants received changes to navigation, communications and warheads, while Moscow developed increasingly sophisticated tactics involving large numbers of attack drones and decoys. That industrial ecosystem is still expanding.
Satellite imagery from early September reportedly shows at least ten new facilities under construction at the Alabuga production complex in Tatarstan. Some of those modifications subsequently appeared in Iranian drones, suggesting that experience accumulated over Ukraine was already flowing back to Tehran.
Some of those modifications subsequently appeared in Iranian drones, suggesting that experience accumulated over Ukraine was already flowing back to Tehran.
“What we are seeing is that military cooperation between Iran and Moscow has not been a one-way street,” Azizi told The New Arab. According to the analyst, Russia has provided Iran with upgrades developed for earlier Shahed variants and information derived from their operational use in Ukraine.
Russian military intelligence cooperation has also contributed to Iranian war efforts, particularly by improving the precision of strikes against US bases in the region.
The missile programme takes this exchange further. Russia is providing expertise accumulated through decades of developing high-speed missiles rather than simply returning Iranian technology in modified form. The specialists involved reportedly included senior Russian engineers working on sea-launched missiles, aerodynamics, ballistics and supersonic ramjet propulsion.
That could have consequences well beyond C430L itself. If Iran masters the propulsion technology, it could potentially incorporate it into later missile designs without requiring Moscow to continuously supply complete weapons. In that sense, the programme points to a broader shift from transactions involving individual weapons systems towards cooperation that can strengthen Iran's own capacity to design, adapt and manufacture them.
A partnership with limits
This does not mean that Russia and Iran have become formal military allies. Their 20-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty signed in January 2025 expanded defence cooperation but stopped short of providing mutual defence guarantees. Moscow has also continued to calibrate its support for Tehran against its relationships elsewhere in the Middle East.
Azizi also distinguishes the relationship from Russia’s partnership with North Korea, which has extended to direct manpower support for Moscow’s war. Iran-Russia cooperation, by comparison, remains concentrated on “technology and intelligence rather than direct assistance”.
The slow progress of the Su-35 programme also illustrates these limits. Tehran has sought the fighters for years and, while recent reporting suggests production is now advancing, their prolonged absence from Iranian service shows how slowly some of the most consequential elements of military cooperation have materialised.
“So this all suggests that there has been a qualitative upgrade in military cooperation between Iran and Russia,” Azizi said. “But it also shows that neither side wants to make it public or go beyond a certain threshold, at least for now.”
C430L fits precisely within that model: strategically valuable, difficult to observe, and capable of strengthening Iran without requiring Russian forces to intervene directly.
Beyond Moscow
Iran’s wartime cooperation is also expanding beyond Russia. The Financial Times investigation places C430L alongside other reported transfers, including Russian Verba man-portable air-defence systems and Iran’s acquisition of a high-resolution Chinese satellite used to monitor US military facilities.
Washington subsequently sanctioned the Chinese supplier Earth Eye, alleging that satellite imagery had supported Iranian strikes against US forces.
Taken together, these developments suggest Tehran is using different relationships to address specific weaknesses exposed during recent conflicts: Russian experience for missile technology and drone development, intelligence cooperation for targeting, and Chinese capabilities for surveillance and other technological requirements.
This does not amount to an emerging trilateral military alliance. Russia and China have different interests in the Middle East, different relationships with Iran and different thresholds for involvement in Tehran's confrontation with Washington. What they do show is Iran's growing ability to draw on separate partnerships for capabilities that its domestic defence sector cannot yet provide on its own.
For Tehran, however, formal alliances may be less important than access. The immediate significance of C430L lies in a missile that could eventually make US naval operations around Iran more dangerous. Its longer-term significance lies in the model behind it.
After years in which Iran supplied Russia with weapons for Ukraine, Moscow is increasingly returning battlefield experience, intelligence, and specialised technological expertise.
If that exchange continues, some of the most consequential Russian weapons transfers to Iran may arrive without a missile ever crossing the border.
Francesco Salesio Schiavi is an Italian specialist in the Middle East. His focus lies in the security architecture of the Levant and the Gulf, with a particular emphasis on Iraq, Iran, and the Arab Peninsula, as well as military and diplomatic interventions by international actors
Follow him on X: @frencio_schiavi

articles.title: Experts: Affordable Munitions Could Help USAF in Taiwan Conflict, but More Is Needed
articles.body:
A new think tank report calls for a buildup of U.S. drones and munitions needed for a potential fight against the Chinese military over Taiwan, thought other experts argue the report is missing some nuance in the munitions equation.
The Center for a New American Security’s report, “Drones, Missiles, and the U.S. Munitions Shortage: The Role of Affordable Mass in a Taiwan Conflict,” released Sept. 18, makes the case for increased long-range weapons to strike Chinese military targets to thwart a takeover of Taiwan.
The report, authored by Philip Sheers and Stacie Pettyjohn, notes a gap between the number of targets the U.S. would need to strike and its diminishing stockpiles, given the ongoing use of such weapons in the conflict with Iran.
“In a U.S.-China conflict over Taiwan that is likely to become protracted, the inventory depth and disruption that lower-cost systems can provide will be invaluable to reversing U.S. disadvantages and stopping China from achieving its operational objectives,” Sheers and Pettyjohn write.
To close the gap, the report recommends both stockpiling high-end missiles and massing cheap drones and munitions to overwhelm a Chinese attack. Other recommendations include:
- Multiyear funding and contracts so manufacturers can expand weapons production capacity and the Pentagon can rebuild long-range missile stores
- Funding for cheap, long-range anti-ship and land-attack weapons to quickly fill inventory gaps.
- Standardized shared components across airframes to lower costs and scale production.
- Pairing inexpensive drones with advanced missiles to drain enemy air defenses.
- Prioritizing easily built designs rather than over-engineering
- Routing updates and briefings to Congress on these issues
The White House and Pentagon have taken steps to boost munitions production this year, especially low-cost weapons.
In July, the Pentagon announced multiyear framework agreements with Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies to mass-produce missiles for the Air Force, followed by a Sept. 17 announcement that Lockheed Martin would expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.
The former announcement is part of USAF’s Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program, unveiled in the fiscal 2026 budget with plans to ramp up such production to hit 5,300 missiles a year by 2028 and reach nearly 8,000 missiles a year by 2031.
The current projected five-year budget for FAMM is more than $12 billion for nearly 27,000 missiles.
Retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, now with AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the CNAS report’s call for more munitions is necessary. But he cautioned that the report’s focus on making weapons affordable needs to be tweaked.
“It should not be about buying cheaper weapons; it should be about how to optimize cost per effect in the battlespace,” Gunzinger said.
The Air Force must fight asymmetrically and maximize the effect of each strike, regardless of munition or platform, and there’s a middle ground for weapons and platform development and procurement, Gunzinger argued.
Precision-guided, specialized weapons such as the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile and the platforms that deliver them are pricey, and lower-end, short-range munitions for stationary targets have their place, but Gunzinger said defense planners can often make too much of a tradeoff if they focus too much on price to the detriment of capability.
“Now you’ve got something that, ‘OK, you hit a price point, but is it going to survive long enough to do its mission?’” Gunzinger said. “Is it going to be able to shoot its weapon before it dies?”
A Numbers Game
The CNAS report’s operational and tactical focus is countering a People’s Liberation Army attack on Taiwan with strikes against PLA ships—destroyers and amphibious assault ships—and hitting airfields on the periphery of the country, close to the Taiwan Strait.
But it does not include a plan to hit the Chinese mainland interior.
“The paper focuses on denying a PLA joint island landing campaign without considering strategic attacks to deny sanctuaries to the PLA and collapse China’s ability to maintain the offensive,” Gunzinger said. “This risks reducing a conflict with the PLA over Taiwan to a force-on-force math problem, like how many weapons and aircraft are needed to attack PLA forces located in the Taiwan Strait and coastal China. It risks becoming a numbers game.”
Because striking mainland China in a Taiwan invasion scenario might be required, Gunzinger said the current 500-nautical-mile limit of most affordable strike options undermines the CNAS report’s conclusion that more mass will equate to victory.
“China has the capability to project outer and inner rings of airborne and sea-based air defense sensors and shooters to defend its cross-Strait forces and operations,” Gunzinger said.
And using nonstealthy drones to approach the Chinese coastline to then launch affordable missiles doesn’t work either, he said. “This would likely result in losses of the aircraft and their weapons.”
“We win part of the battle,” Gunzinger said. “They win the war.”
Breaking a Stalemate
The numbers-on-numbers approach is what has led to a stalemate in the Russia-Ukraine War, said retired Navy Cmdr. J. Michael Dahm, now a senior fellow for aerospace and China studies at Mitchell.
“Just because you can generate mass doesn’t mean that you’re going to achieve your effects,” Dahm told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “You may be able to keep your adversary off balance, but if you’re not going to then judo throw him into what you want him to do, you’re just engaging in this kind of protracted, endless warfare.”
Throughout the history of the modern Chinese military, it has mostly been defense-oriented, Dahm said. The PLA has airfields dotting its landscape and hardened sites to pull and rotate forces from, as well as a layered air defense network.
What could overwhelm the Chinese defenses, however, is what the U.S. has seen poke through its defenses recently in the Middle East, Dahm said. Iranian air attacks have used a combination of low-end munitions and cheap drones with more expensive and capable missiles fired from various angles, locations, and at varying rates of speed to confuse and defeat air defenses.
This aligns with one of the report’s recommendations—for the Pentagon to develop new operational concepts that pair cheap and high-end weapons for mixed attacks.
“Using low-cost drones in the opening wave to identify air defenses, consume interceptors, and relay targeting data to follow-on missiles offers a promising and sustainable way to create repeated air base disruption,” according to the report. “High-end weapons should be preserved for more challenging targets, while affordable mass should be integrated into strike plans to service soft targets and to saturate air defenses.”
“The Iranians have figured out how to be effective: … send a whole bunch of slow-moving drones with a couple of cruise missiles and a couple of ballistic missiles,” Dahm said.
That’s because modern air defenders must set their systems to track certain ranges, altitudes, and speeds of whatever is in the airspace. And they can’t track everything effectively all at once.
“I don’t want a flock of birds showing up on my radar, so I set the speed gate for higher speed, but how high do I set it for? 100 knots or do I set it for Mach 3? What am I looking for? Range. How far am I looking? Altitude. Am I looking high? Am I looking low?” Dahm said.
Those factors mean an air defense system can’t stop everything.
“The way you overwhelm even the most sophisticated air defense system is you send some slow stuff, you send some medium stuff, and then you send these ballistic missiles that are screaming in from the upper atmosphere at Mach 3-4-5,” Dahm said. “It is hard for any modern air defense system to deal with all those inputs.”
While Iran is using that method against the U.S., Dahm advocates the U.S. use the same strategy in a Taiwan scenario against the PLA.
“That is absolutely what we should be doing,” Dahm said.
For example, to strike a Chinese military ship, such as a cruiser, Dahm said U.S. or coalition countries wouldn’t only send the same type of missile from one direction. They would simultaneously target the ship from air, land, sea, and subsurface platforms with a variety of projectiles at varying speeds and ranges, though the centerpiece of the assault might be an LRASM.
“You might send two LRASMs, but you need to accompany that with some of these more cost-effective missiles,” he said. “It is the reason we need the cost-effectiveness and the affordability, because we shouldn’t have an expectation that all of those weapons are going to work.”

articles.title: Russian Drones Over Kyiv – War of Speed and New Deep Strike Tactics
articles.body:
Russia’s “Shahed / Geran” drones are attacking Ukraine’s civilian cities almost continuously. Their targets of choice include shopping malls, gas stations, energy infrastructure, food warehouses, office centers and other civilian facilities. They increasingly deploy jet-powered Geran 4 and 5 variants of the drones that have replaced the so-called “mopeds” – powered by piston engines.
Ukraine recorded around 180 uses of jet-powered drones in the whole of 2025. In August this year alone, they launched around 2,800 – Russia used 15 times the annual total of jet-powered drones in a single month. Russia’s once experimental weapon, that it occasionally launched to test Ukraine’s air-defense capabilities is now one of mass deployment.
nd this creates new challenges for Ukraine. Having learned relatively quickly to effectively intercept conventional Shaheds – open-source data shows interception rates reached 90-95%. These jet-powered targets present a more complicated challenge for Ukraine with currently only around 60% interception rates.
The success Russia is currently achieving with jet-powered drones clearly demonstrates one of the fundamental principles of modern warfare – the race to implement new technologies faster than the enemy. Each side constantly probes the other’s vulnerabilities and can rapidly scale up a technology or tactic that works.
Russian Drone Attack on Kyiv Kills 2, Injures 22 as Explosions Rock Central Kyiv
Changes in Russian tactics
Russia has not simply increased the number of attacks; it has constantly changed how those attacks are conducted. These changes likely have several objectives: to overwhelm Ukraine’s air-defense system, forcing it to use expensive missiles against relatively cheap targets, create prolonged panic, and ultimately identify areas where Ukrainian defenses are weaker.
Where Ukraine’s defenses are thinnest, Russia tries to scale up its attacks. Constant attacks on civilian as well as military infrastructure in major cities serve to disrupt the functioning of the country. When air-raid alerts last for hours, logistics are disrupted, people move to shelters and businesses suspend operations. Even if a drone does not hit its target, the threat itself creates an economic impact and reduces the country’s financial capacity.
This effect is especially visible in Kyiv. When air-raid alerts are repeatedly declared, the capital simply cannot operate in a normal way which, in my view, is one of Moscow’s objectives: not simply to destroy something, but to gradually paralyze normal life. Russia is also trying to destroy residents’ morale by striking warehouses in an attempt to cause shortages and disruption to food and other essential supplies.
There is another aspect to these air attacks. They do not necessarily have to end with a strike against a specific target. The use of aircraft for reconnaissance can provide data about Ukraine’s response: where and how air defenses operate, which routes are being blocked, how quickly Ukraine responds to a target, and which systems are used to intercept it.
Even though not every drone launched by Russia is designed to explode, the objective ultimately remains the same: to destroy Ukraine.
Energy infrastructure, military and government facilities, communications towers, telecommunications infrastructure, media offices, gas stations, shopping malls – the list of potential targets is endless. Drones can be manually controlled and switch between targets in real time.
Every single attack can serve several purposes simultaneously: inflicting physical damage, overwhelming air defenses, collecting intelligence or simply keeping up constant psychological pressure. Nighttime attacks disrupt sleep and reduce productivity of Ukrainians throughout the following working day.
Why jet-powered drones are difficult to Intercept?
Conventional Shaheds fly relatively slowly allowing Ukraine’s air-defense forces time to detect them and assign the appropriate weapon system to destroy them. A jet-powered that flies twice as fast or more aircraft significantly reduces that window.
Speed is not the only factor; flight altitude, trajectory, terrain, buildings and the number of simultaneous targets present air defense with an entirely different and more complex problem.
Jet-powered drones operate at altitudes above 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles), meaning that some of the conventional tools – mobile fire teams, machine guns, Gepard anti-aircraft systems and MANPADS – become ineffective. This leaves three main tools: fighter aircraft, surface-to-air missile systems and interceptor drones.
Russia does not rely on a single design with various types of jet-powered drones emerging, with some already approaching the capabilities of cruise missiles.
The Geran-5, for example, reportedly has a range of around 950 kilometers (590 miles) and a warhead of up to 90 kilograms (198 pounds). The Bandrol develops a speed of approximately 500-560 km/h (310-350 mph) and can go even faster during an attacking dive. The Dan-T drone-missile has a payload of up to 135 kilograms (298 pounds).
“Mother Drones” – another new Russian tactic
Recent attacks on Kyiv involved the use of so-called “mother drones.” These are Shaheds acting as carriers for smaller, faster and more maneuverable first-person view (FPV) drones which are released closer to and can be directed on to a potential target deep behind the front lines – distances that would otherwise be beyond the FPV drone.
The limited use of the tactic so far suggests it is yet another Russian testbed prior to mass deployment
What new threats could emerge?
Ukrainian defense engineers today must identify trends, understand the direction of technological evolution, and anticipate the direction Russian technology might take and develop countermeasures before they become a “game changer.”
When assessing the threat, it is not just technical or tactical capability that is important – scale. We have already seen that Russia was able to rapidly increase the production of relatively inexpensive guided munitions. It is not solely important to be able to effectively intercept a particular target but also in sufficient numbers.
Even the world’s best interceptor will not suffice if production is limited while the enemy can manufacture thousands of cheaper targets.
We need asymmetry.
The countermeasure should preferably cost significantly less than the target it faces or Ukraine could literally be exhausted by the financial cost of war. Ideally Ukraine should make mass attacks economically unattractive to Russia.
The future will be largely defined by a war of quantity – more missiles, more UAVs, more types of munitions opposed by more countermeasures – with lower cost being essential for both offensive and defensive systems.
Just as essential as quantity and price alone the decisive advantage will see a struggle for quality and autonomy with artificial intelligence (AI) inevitably becoming part of that process.
As the number and type of munitions increase, they will by necessity become “smarter,” requiring fewer external commands for guidance. They will be able to analyze their surroundings, adjust their routes, and independently select the moment or direction from which to approach a target.
With hundreds or thousands of different targets flying simultaneously, it will be impossible to train and field the same numbers of pilots. Both sides will rely on decisions being delegated to algorithms.
AI will be used to both strike targets and launch countermeasures. Systems will be able to analyze the airspace more quickly, predict flight paths, filter out decoys, allocate weapons to genuine targets, and operate without constant human intervention.
Future warfare will increasingly see humans defining the rules, while machines perform most of the work. This is already happening in civilian life. Vehicles can now operate without drivers, and AI systems are capable of independently analyzing enormous volumes of information. The next logical step is greater autonomy in military systems.
What Ukraine needs to do to protect its skies
The technological race is already underway – at full speed. If Ukraine is not to lose, it needs to prepare for this race now.
In 2023, when the first Shaheds appeared Ukraine could only counter them effectively by using expensive missiles, which were already in short supply. Kyiv went through a rapid and productive evolution – from detecting drones with searchlights to effectively destroying them over Ukraine. When conventional “mopeds” stopped delivering the results Russia needed, jet-powered unmanned aircraft began to appear.
Ukraine cannot afford to simply catch up with Russia every time it introduces a new technology. It needs to develop its own solutions in advance – both offensive systems and countermeasures. In no time at all fast, high-flying drones will be able to independently decide where to fly, what to attack and how to circumvent its defenses.
Several Ukrainian companies are already developing and combat testing jet-powered interceptor drones. The next steps will be scaling up production which should significantly improve Ukraine’s ability to intercept jet-powered UAVs.
Ukraine needs to think more broadly. It needs domestic production of jet engines and to avoid becoming dependent on third countries, including China. Similarly it should also increase the number of radars, protection for aircraft and strike drone bases and production facilities to manufacture its own jet-powered drones combined with strong intelligence capabilities and sufficient strike assets.
At the same time, Ukraine will have to adapt to the new reality of round-the-clock air threats and attacks. It is impossible to live for months in a situation where every air-raid siren automatically means a complete halt to normal life. It needs a much more precise system for understanding where the danger actually exists and how immediate it is. Where life can safely continue, the country should keep working. Where there is an immediate threat, people should receive a clear warning and be able to move to shelters.
Kyiv has already introduced different levels of air-raid alert. The same principle applies not only to protection, but to active defense as well. This calls for the introduction of a range of countermeasures as new types of target appear. Air-defense effectiveness is not only about the number of targets destroyed but also the cost of interception.
If an attacking munition costs $10,000 while the defensive system used to destroy it costs $100,000, the engagement may be won but the overall economic race will be lost.
Electronic warfare is another critical element of this development. For example, BlueBird Tech is constantly improving its Hrets systems in close cooperation with the military to respond quickly, because tactics and technologies are changing every day. As long as electronic communications exist, there will be ways to detect, intercept, jam or protect against them. Even if some systems become autonomous, warfare will not become fully automated overnight.
In addition electronic warfare itself will gradually move toward greater automation. Systems will be able to analyze the electromagnetic spectrum independently, identify signals, determine their source and select an appropriate response. AI will be an integral part of the electronic warfare system itself.
However, it is important to understand that Russia will not stop with jet-powered drones. By the time we learn how to intercept them effectively, Moscow may already have the next iteration: cheaper weapons, greater numbers, new tactics or increased autonomy.
Ukraine’s task, therefore, is not simply to catch up with every new threat as it emerges. It is to build a system capable of adapting faster than the adversary – and staying one step ahead.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy ready for ‘energy ceasefire’, as Nato warns Putin becoming ‘increasingly cavalier’
articles.body:
- 
  Volodymyr Zelenskyy discussed with Donald Trump on Tuesday efforts to end the 4-year-old war with Russia, including a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets. “We are ready for any kind of format of energy ceasefire” if Russia agrees to “not attack our energy system,” Zelenskyy told journalists after meeting with Trump at the UN headquarters in New York. The Ukrainian leader expressed hope the “American side will find a way … to bring them to any kind of negotiations.” Zelenskyy said that he also was ready to meet the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, at a trilateral meeting with Trump.
- 
  Trump insisted he was working with both sides to end the war, despite little evidence of Putin being open to any settlement. “It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand,” Trump said in his UN speech. Efforts led by Washington to broker a deal to end the hostilities, which have raged since Russia launched its all-out invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, have stalled in recent months as the US has shifted focus to its war against Iran.
- 
  Zelenskyy claimed the war with Russia would end if Trump applied more pressure on Putin, and if China and India stop buying oil from Russia. “It’s enough to stop them, they will not have enough money,” Zelenskyy told The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday. Zelenskyy said Russia’s energy sales to China, India and Turkey were propping up Russia’s economy. During the same interview, Zelenskyy said that Trump on Tuesday did not ask him to stop bombing Russian oil refineries. However, he acknowledged the issue has been raised before by American partners over concerns of rising energy prices.
- 
  Zelenskyy also met with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, in New York, who said he lobbied Trump to press for a Ukraine-Russia energy ceasefire in his meeting with his Ukrainian counterpart. Burnham promised further financial support to Kyiv for infrastructure.
- 
  Putin is becoming “increasingly cavalier, dangerous and risk accepting,” as his war in Ukraine drags on and as he seeks to divide western allies, Nato’s deputy commander in Europe said Tuesday. Air Chief Marshal Sir John Stringer spoke to The Associated Press at a security conference in Estonia amid warnings from some European leaders that Moscow is planning to test Nato’s collective defence pact with bolder attacks that have already included sabotage and espionage. Stringer warned that Nato members need to be aware of the “febrile environment” and be careful in their response because Putin would like to provoke the alliance into an “overreaction”.
- 
  Officials in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which border Russia, have been more cautious about the prospect of a serious escalation. “Ukraine is fighting. Russia is absorbed in Ukraine. We do not observe any buildup near our borders. And from that part, I think that most would agree that the perspective of direct military attack is not correct,” Latvian president Edgars Rinkevics told reporters on the sidelines of the UN meeting. European countries have already faced multiple incursions of Russian drones – and several missiles – as well as a campaign of covert Russian disruption which began after the war.
- 
  Ukraine has continued to press the US for more Patriot interceptors to defend against Russia’s ballistic missiles, but is yet to get any confirmation, Zelenskyy told reporters. “They are positive to help us, but I didn’t get the very concrete answer,” he said. Defence experts say the US has been experiencing a global shortage of Patriot interceptors because many have been expended to defend against Iranian attacks on US and allied bases in Middle East. Zelenskyy spoke of the urgency of needing the weapons, which can shoot down Russia’s more advanced ballistic missiles. The shortage in Ukraine has left Kyiv and other cities increasingly exposed to devastating attacks.

articles.title: The United States and South Korea agreed to help resume dialogue with Pyongyang
articles.body:
The United States and South Korea agreed to help resume dialogue with Pyongyang
Kyiv • UNN
Lee Jae-myung and Donald Trump agreed to help resume dialogue with Pyongyang. Seoul seeks to initiate talks on peace and denuclearization.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and U.S. President Donald Trump agreed to work closely to help restore dialogue with North Korea, with Trump once again expressing his willingness to engage in talks with Kim Jong Un. Bloomberg reports, according to UNN.
Details
Both leaders said they would maintain close contact as they worked to resume negotiations with Pyongyang and establish lasting peace on the Korean Peninsula, South Korean National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac said. According to him, Lee and Trump met for approximately 30 minutes in New York on Tuesday evening.
The agreement was reached after Lee called in his address to the UN General Assembly for the swiftest possible resumption of talks between the United States and North Korea, seeking to leverage Trump's relationship with Kim to overcome the peninsula's years-long deadlock.
Calling Trump the person who created a "hard-to-reach opportunity for change," Lee said that South Korea would lay the groundwork for holding new talks "as soon as possible."
Trump, who met with Kim several times during his first presidential term but ultimately failed to reach a deal, has repeatedly said that he is ready to speak with the North Korean leader again. Kim has so far rejected these proposals.
Lee said that South Korea would work to turn any renewed talks between the United States and North Korea into full-fledged negotiations aimed at officially ending the Korean War and establishing peace. South Korea is formally still at war with nuclear-armed North Korea, as the 1950–1953 conflict ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty.
Lee outlined a new approach under which North Korea would first halt the expansion of its nuclear and missile capabilities, then reduce them in the medium term, and ultimately move toward a denuclearized Korean Peninsula in the long term. This represents a departure from the demand that Kim immediately give up his nuclear weapons—a strategy that led to the failure of Trump's last substantive talks with Kim in Vietnam in 2019.
Supplement
Despite numerous UN sanctions, North Korea is now capable of producing enough weapons-grade nuclear material to create up to 20 nuclear warheads per year, Lee said in January. Kim's regime, which has declared itself a nuclear state, is now less isolated than at any time in recent decades. This is evidenced, among other things, by the mutual defense treaty concluded with Russia in 2024, under which North Korea is helping Moscow in its war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Trump threatens Iran with ‘hell’ at UN, predicts deal after US midterm elections
articles.body:
President Donald Trump used his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday to defend an increasingly interventionist foreign policy, casting himself as a leader willing to use American military, diplomatic and economic power while declaring that the United States would continue to put its own interests first.
“While others have talked, I have acted,” Trump said. “While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them.”
Much of the speech focused on Iran and the nearly seven-month war that has reshaped the Middle East and disrupted global energy markets. Trump defended his decision to go to war alongside Israel earlier this year and said Tehran had rejected previous efforts to reach an agreement that would prevent it from obtaining nuclear weapons.
Trump said he now faced what he called a “big decision” over whether to reach a deal that would allow Iran to recover or move toward far more destructive military action.
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he asked, before saying he nevertheless expected an agreement after the November midterm elections.
Trump said Iranian leaders were waiting to see how Republicans performed in the midterms, though he stressed that he himself was not on the ballot.
“The Republican Party is running, and I’m going to help them,” he said, adding that his principal concern remained ensuring that Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon.
He also rejected reports that concerns over depleted US ammunition and interceptor stocks were constraining his military options, saying the United States possessed large quantities of weapons and was replenishing them rapidly.
Trump called on other countries to join Washington in economically isolating Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping, abandons its nuclear ambitions and stops supporting terrorism.
The war with Iran has complicated Trump’s effort to portray his foreign policy as a series of successful peace interventions. The Wall Street Journal reported that the White House is seeking to present his international record as a collection of tangible wins for Americans ahead of the midterms, even as the wars involving Iran and Ukraine continue to weigh on energy prices and global trade.
Trump invokes Oct. 7 and Gaza deal
Trump also invoked Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, accusing Iran of supporting the terrorists responsible and arguing that Tehran could never be permitted to operate under the protection of a nuclear arsenal.
He said Iran’s supreme leader had celebrated the massacre and described the threat posed by a nuclear-armed Islamic Republic as one the United States could not ignore.
Trump then pointed to Gaza as evidence of what he described as his ability to turn conflict into negotiated outcomes.
He recalled that when he addressed the General Assembly a year earlier, the Gaza war was still underway and hostages remained in Hamas captivity. His administration’s 20-point plan was later endorsed by the UN Security Council, and the Board of Peace was established to oversee the postwar framework. The board says the ceasefire brought the return of all hostages and is now focused on demilitarization, Palestinian civilian administration, reconstruction and humanitarian assistance.
Trump thanked Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and other countries contributing to Gaza, saying their money was reaching areas where humanitarian needs remain acute.
He also praised countries that have committed personnel, police or training to Gaza stabilization efforts, including Indonesia, Morocco, Albania, Kosovo, Kazakhstan, Egypt and Jordan.
The Board of Peace is scheduled to meet on the sidelines of the General Assembly to review implementation of the Gaza framework and discuss its next priorities.
Ukraine, Greenland and Venezuela next
Trump devoted less time to Russia’s war against Ukraine, saying his administration was continuing efforts to bring the conflict to an end.
His diplomatic agenda after the speech underscored how much unfinished business remains.
He was scheduled to meet separately with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Gulf leaders, with the Iran war expected to feature prominently in the regional discussions. The continuing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine have both contributed to pressure on global energy markets.
Trump was also expected to sign an agreement expanding the US military and commercial presence in Greenland after nearly two years of pressure on Denmark, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Another meeting was set with Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, whose government has entered into an arrangement giving the Pentagon a stake in the country’s oil sector. Trump has argued that closer US involvement in Venezuelan energy production will help lower fuel prices at home.
The meeting is politically sensitive because Rodríguez was a senior figure in the government of Nicolás Maduro, who was removed in a US military operation earlier this year. Trump has emphasized cooperation with Rodríguez while moving more slowly on a transition to democratic government, according to the Journal.
Xi summit looms
Trump’s UN appearance also comes on the eve of a three-day state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The two leaders are expected to discuss artificial intelligence, rare earth minerals and Taiwan, among other issues. The Journal reported that Trump, who previously took a more confrontational approach toward Beijing, is now seeking a less adversarial relationship and wants to avoid a deepening economic and military confrontation.
The summit is expected to focus heavily on optics and the broader relationship rather than major new agreements.
Trump’s packed schedule reflects the contrast at the heart of his UN message: he presented himself as a president who has already delivered peace through decisive action, even as some of the largest crises he has confronted remain unresolved.
His Iran policy captures that tension most clearly. Trump threatened Tehran with potentially devastating consequences while simultaneously predicting that diplomacy would ultimately prevail.
“The president is open to a meeting with him or anybody,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian ahead of the speech, while cautioning that Iran’s supreme leader remains the country’s ultimate decision-maker.
For Trump, the message to the General Assembly was that willingness to negotiate and willingness to use force are not contradictory elements of his foreign policy.
“While others have spoken of peace,” he told world leaders, “I have made peace.”

articles.title: North Korea's Kim lauds test of apparent new hypersonic missile
articles.body:
North Korea's Kim Jong Un lauds apparent hypersonic missile test, calls it "incurable headache" for foes
Hong Kong — With his teenage daughter and possible successor by his side, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un watched on Sunday as his country tested a purported new hypersonic weapon designed to evade missile defenses. North Korean state media said Kim had lauded the weapon as an "irresistible force" that would be an "incurable headache" for North Korea's adversaries.
The country's state-run KCNA news agency said the "new weapon" tested on Sunday was "of great significance."
The type of weapon was not specified by the reports, but photographs released by KCNA showed Kim, with his daughter Kim Ju Ae, inspecting a screen with a label reading, "Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory."
Analysts say the title suggests the test was of an upgraded version of an existing North Korean short-range ballistic missile that adds a retrofitted hypersonic glide vehicle. Hypersonic missiles can generally fly lower and faster than conventional rockets, making them more difficult to intercept. North Korea has tested various hypersonic weapons systems since 2021.
They are among the advanced weapons Kim has wanted his country to develop as he seeks to upgrade North Korea's nuclear capabilities.
The test launch on Sunday will come as a blow to South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who is expected to lay out plans to improve relations with Pyongyang at the U.N. General Assembly this week. The two Koreas have remained technically at war since fighting in the Korean War ended in 1953 with a ceasefire agreement rather than a full peace deal.
Lee has proposed dropping South Korea's longstanding demand for Pyongyang to give up its nuclear weapons as a precondition for talks, suggesting instead a freeze on further nuclear weapons testing or development by North Korea, at least initially.
President Trump has also repeatedly expressed interest in meeting with Kim, possibly around the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November. The White House has suggested that talks could be held "without any preconditions."
Mr. Trump met with Kim three times during his first term, but failed to make any progress on the issue of denuclearization. Since then, North Korea has continued to develop its nuclear and conventional weapons programs and is now believed to possess dozens of nuclear warheads.
South Korea's government claims Pyongyang has between 80 and 120 warheads. Mr. Trump recently said the North had 57 nuclear warheads.
The Kim regime has given no indication of interest in a new round of talks with Mr. Trump or with Lee, despite Mr. Trump's move last month to scale back annual military drills with South Korea, which he called "hostile" to Pyongyang.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Reportedly to Request Patriot Missiles, Propose Energy Truce in UN Talks with Trump
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Zelenskyy Reportedly to Request Patriot Missiles, Propose Energy Truce in UN Talks with Trump
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where he plans to push for a mutual energy ceasefire with Russia, Reuters reported on September 22.
The high-stakes meeting comes as Ukrainians brace for intensified Russian winter attacks on their domestic heating and power grids.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In a post on X on September 21, Zelenskyy expressed cautious optimism following a phone call with Trump, noting “diplomatic momentum” and proposing that if Russia ceases attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector and food exports, Ukraine will take “matching de-escalation steps.”
In recent weeks, both nations have ramped up aerial campaigns, with Russian strikes battering Ukrainian port facilities and energy infrastructure, while Ukraine has successfully responded by crippling portions of Russia’s vital oil refining industry through long-range drone strikes, Reuters wrote.
For Trump, the diplomatic push is heavily influenced by domestic politics, according to Reuters. Facing low approval ratings and soaring global diesel and gas prices just weeks before the November midterm elections, Trump has been highly critical of the Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries.
Reuters reports that Trump posted on Truth Social on September 21 that “Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil industry due to its War with Ukraine,” adding that “the whole World suffers” and calling for an end to the war.
According to sources familiar with the discussions who spoke to Reuters, Trump has directly asked Zelenskyy to halt the refinery attacks. However, Kyiv remains reluctant to abandon its deep-strike campaign—which recently forced the shutdown of a major Moscow refinery—viewing the systemic damage to Russia’s lucrative energy sector as its strongest leverage to force Moscow to negotiate.
The prospects for a lasting energy truce remain highly unlikely. Trump claimed last week that both sides had agreed to stop striking energy targets, but that arrangement evaporated within a day after Russia bombed petrol stations in Kyiv and Ukraine retaliated against Russian oil infrastructure, Reuters noted.
Critics also note that Trump’s push for an energy truce in Ukraine serves as a deflection from his administration’s war with Iran, which has significantly spiked global oil prices.
If Russia refuses to de-escalate, Reuters notes that Zelenskyy is expected to pivot the discussion toward securing more US-made Patriot air defense missiles, which are currently in severe short supply worldwide, to counter Russia’s escalating barrage of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones ahead of the winter freeze.
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps had recently destroyed a key fuel pipeline running from Russia’s Voronezh region that supplied 50% of the daily diesel for Russian troops in occupied Luhansk. The strike forced Russian supply trucks on a 400-kilometer detour back into Russia for fuel, triggering immediate shortages that disrupted frontline drone operations and electronic warfare systems.
