articles.title: Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
A relative pause in fighting between the United States and Iran that ended in early September has brought the region back into a state of geopolitical tension.
As the exchange of strikes, retaliations, and signalling between Washington and Tehran continues, there is a heightened expectation from Washington that the US pullout from Iraq should coincide with Iranian-backed militias in the country being disarmed.
A looming US withdrawal
At a meeting at the White House in July, Iraq’s new prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, met with President Donald Trump and indicated that Baghdad would work to disarm the pro-Iranian Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF).
“The fact that both Trump and Zaidi are following through means this is a bipartisan vision in the United States and a continued commitment from Zaidi, who took over the premiership from Sudani as the Coordination Framework’s candidate,” Hamzeh Hadad, an Adjunct Fellow with the Center for New American Security, told The New Arab.
The withdrawal of US forces now places a greater burden on the government in Baghdad to determine the future of the PMF.
“The US pullout removes a key lever for Baghdad and forces tougher bargaining at home,” Dr Inna Rudolf, Senior Research Fellow in the War Studies Department at King’s College London, told The New Arab.
“Coalition forces had been both an excuse some factions used for pursuing greater autonomy but also a tool Washington could use to push for change.”
The US continues to pressure Baghdad for the disarmament of the PMF through diplomatic channels, but the threat of further sanctions and tariffs has been floated by the Trump administration.
On 21 September, Zaidi requested more time beyond the 30 September deadline agreed with the United States, and the next day it was announced that it would be pushed back to 30 June 2027.
Baghdad will now have nine months to continue negotiations with the factions while avoiding potential US financial or economic sanctions.
“The Iraqi government needs to have a more honest dialogue with Washington about its situation and vision,” Haddad told The New Arab.
“But this needs to take place without wishful statements from the Iraqi side that they backtrack on, as they already have to deal with strong foreign pressure on the issue.”
The plan to dismantle and reorganise the PMF fighters into existing brigades and retire older commanders who have served since 2014 will reportedly start implementation in January 2027.
The government also intends to establish a new directorate to monitor the integration.
Zaidi's disarmament push
Iraq’s new prime minister has sought to strengthen Baghdad’s image as a government that can rein in corruption, ensure security, and pursue economic development with the international community.
“Zaidi, entering politics, a new face, with no prior experience in public office, wanted to build on the US backing that saw him come to power, and so he boldly stated that he would enforce a deadline for armed groups outside of the state apparatus to disarm,” said Hadad.
The Iraqi government is currently waging a campaign to curtail the PMF’s power in the country. In mid-August, Iraqi security forces detained a senior commander from the Nujaba Movement, one of the primary Iranian-backed militias that make up the PMF coalition.
“There is a different understanding between what constitutes armed groups outside of the state apparatus in Iraq than in Washington,” Hadad noted.
Hiba Abdulwahhab, an Iraqi researcher and analyst, told The New Arab, “The relationship between the Iraqi government and these factions resembles a Catholic marriage, a union with no easy divorce. They are deeply intertwined politically, institutionally, and economically”.
An uncertain security situation
The US military will also be removing the air defence systems, including Patriot and C-RAM systems, from the Kurdistan Region. The depletion of US air defence system interceptors during the conflict with Iran has contributed to the declining security situation.
In March 2026, Kataib Hezbollah, one of the key factions of the PMF, released a two-minute video that went viral showing an FPV drone flying over the Camp Victory complex near Baghdad International Airport, a site that continued to host US and NATO-linked facilities.
A drone attack that Saudi officials reported originated from Iraq struck the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia on 11 September. Baghdad later confirmed the pipeline attack came from Iraqi territory and dismissed security officials responsible for Maysan Province near the Iranian border and closed the area’s border crossing.
Still, some PMF groups have sought out a political advantage by appearing to adhere to the government’s calls. One militia, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, announced over the summer that it formally withdrew from the PMF coalition and handed over its weapons to the government.
Other groups, such as the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades and the Nujaba Movement, have stated they will not turn over their weapons, saying that certain conditions had to be met before they did so.
“[Zaidi’s] reasoning is that there will be no more American forces present in Iraq and therefore no more excuse for armed groups to exist after that,” Hadad told The New Arab.
Dr Rudolf agrees. “Losing that pretext gives negotiators cleaner rhetorical space to press for stricter control as it strips the factions of their usual talking point that foreign troops justify armed resistance outside the formal chain of command.”
Finding a path to disarmament
Iraqi leaders have advocated for the PMF to function as a state security institution and slowly reduce their political nature.
In May, the militia of prominent Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, Saraya al-Salam, announced it would begin disarmament and integrate into the state. While this group is not technically part of the PMF and Shia Coordination Framework, it could be interpreted as a sign of the direction the wind is blowing in Iraq.
However, it is likely that the groups will utilise this approach to reposition themselves without totally surrendering their arms.
“The most likely outcome is therefore adaptation and repositioning rather than genuine disarmament,” Abdulwahhab told The New Arab.
“Weapons could remain in faction-controlled depots, be transferred to affiliated units, or be placed nominally within the PMF’s official structure without being brought under effective government command.”
Observers of Iraq are right to be sceptical that the PMF will do little else other than rebrand and retain their loyalty to informal chains of command and external ties with Tehran.
Regarding the extension of the disarmament deadline, Abdulwahhab said, “The progression raises serious doubts about the government’s ability to act against factions deeply embedded in Iraq’s political and security institutions”.
She added, “The extension is more likely to give Iran-aligned factions time to reorganise and protect their networks than to give the government the power to disarm and dismantle them,” further noting that Baghdad had to take concrete steps now, otherwise June 2027 may bring another postponement rather than a resolution.
Some positive steps have been taken, but it is still early in the process to understand how far Baghdad can go.
“Without tangible incentives and accountability mechanisms, ‘integration’ will feel like administrative rebranding,” Rudolf said. “The public will see it as window dressing.”
The long-term outlook will depend on the future of the financial and military support from Iran as well as Baghdad’s own ability to assert control over the militias.
For now, the government in Baghdad will have to navigate the post-US withdrawal environment on its own.
Christopher Solomon is a Middle East analyst, researcher, editor, and writer based in the Washington, DC area. He is the author of the book In Search of Greater Syria (Bloomsbury)
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Davey says far right in Britain now better funded and supported than in the past – UK politics live
articles.body:
Trump says his relationship with UK better now with Burnham as PM than with Starmer
Donald Trump was being polite and respectful for most of the very short press conference he held with Andy Burnham, but towards the end he could not resist a jibe about Keir Starmer.
Asked about UK-US relations by a reporter who said they had gone up and down, Trump replied:
No I think they’re up.
Well they’re more up now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.
I think right now, based on my relationship with the prime minister, Andy, I think that, I think we’re doing very well.
At one point the relationship between Trump and Starmer was good. But it got worse as Starmer started to criticise Trump publicly on issues like his proposal to annex Greenland, and his claim British troops avoided frontline action in Afghanistan. And the full rupture came when Keir Starmer refused to allow the US to use British airbases for attacks against Iran at the start of the war.
Burnham defends sanctions on West Bank settlements, as Trump does not criticise and claims to be unaware of details
At the press conference, Andy Burnham also defended the decision to impose sanctions on the West Bank settlements.
A US reporter asked Donald Trump what he thought about this. Trump claimed that he did not know about this. He asked Burnham if he knew about it.
And Burnham replied:
Yes. Obviously we took that decision, the foreign secretary [Ed Miliband] and I. And we did call you just to say why we had taken that.
I take this view on this issue. We have all spoken over the years about the importance of the two-state solution. If we face the situation where there is a tender on the West Bank that in effect make a two-state solution non-viable, what do we do? Because if we do nothing, then if further erodes people’s trust in politics, hey think you’re all talks, when it comes to it you are not prepared to follow up on that talk and do something.
Burnham said he condemned the Hamas attacks on 7 October “completely”.
But politicians had to show there was meaning behind their words, he said.
Trump backs Burnham after PM says he wants to give UK a 'positive story' and 'hopefulness'
In response to a question about whether he was happier in Manchester of Manhatten at the short, 12-minute press conference, Andy Burnham talked about the great city of Manchester and referred to Donald Trump once calling it a “town”. Burnham went on, jokingly: “We don’t, I don’t hold it against you, as the former mayor.”
Burnham said he loved the US too.
And he launched into a riff about patriotism.
I was explaining to the president today, Britain has been in too much turbulence, a sense of us not know where were are going. And I think you responded when I said we’re going to lay out a plan for Britain, 10-year direction.
The country’s got so much going for it. And it’s time to turn the story about Britain to a positive story, get some hopefulness going around the country.
And I think you were saying today that very much is how you see it.
Trump said he agreed. He said there was a tremendous patriotism about Britain. And he joked about it having “got more names than any other place in the world”, because some people called it Britain, and some the United Kingdom, and some England.
He said it was just “waiting for good leadership, waiting for success”.
'We've done a great job' - Trump defends his record in Iran
At the press conference the Guardian’s Pippa Crerar asked Donald Trump if he expected UK to help him if he chose to annihilate Iran. And she asked if he had any sympathy for the allies are suffering because of rising petrol prices due to the war.
Trump did not really engage with any of her points.
Instead, he gave quite a rambling answer, saying:
I think as soon as the war is over, the numbers are going to come way down, pricing generally.
Oil is the big thing when the oil goes up.
And we had to do that because we have to stop them. And I think we feel very united on that. We can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.
And people understand that in the United States, and they’re paying less than Biden, by the way, less than the Biden administration. And yet he did nothing about the threat of nuclear terror.
It’s nuclear terror. We can’t have it. So we’ve stopped them from having a nuclear weapon. We’ve literally stopped them. They’re not going to have a nuclear weapon. And we’ll see what happens.
I think that a settlement is going to be reached. They want to talk to us. They have been talking to us, even today. The relationship is developing, let’s say.
But we can’t let them … have a nuclear weapon. And there’s a price to pay for that.
This should have been done by other presidents. Or, frankly, other countries. Some country could have stepped forward. But there aren’t too many countries, frankly, that could have handled that.
So I think we’ve done a great job. They will not have a nuclear weapon.
Yesterday Andy Burnham spoke to the prime minister of Mauritius, Navin Ramgoolam, This is what Downing Street said in the readout of the call about what was said about the Chagos Islands deal.
Turning to the future of the military base on Diego Garcia, the prime minister underlined his commitment to working with Mauritius and the United States on a way forward that secures the operation of the base and protects UK national security.
And this is what Nigel Farage, who has been urging Donald Trump to block the Chagos Islands deal for about a year, posted on social media tonight after Trump’s comments. (See 6.20pm.)
Trump describes Chagos Islands deal as 'terrible', and claims Burnham has agreed to review it
Donald Trump described the Chagos Islands deal – a proposal by Keir Starmer’s goverment to give Mauritius sovereignty over the Chagos Islands, on condition that the US and the UK can continue to operate the Diego Garcia military base there for at least another 99 years – as “terrible”.
In the short press conference with Burnham, Trump said:
I don’t support it. I think it’s a terrible deal.
They all of a sudden say they have ownership, somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous. No, we were talking about that.
It’s strategically very important, very important. You know, we had to send our B-2 bombers when we bombed the Iran nuclear, we sent the B-2 bombers back home to Missouri. As opposed to flying for a short period of time, they had to fly for a long period of time.
It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it. It’s very strategic location. And it’s unique
It’s a very important piece of real estate, militarily and strategically.
Trump says his relationship with UK better now with Burnham as PM than with Starmer
Donald Trump was being polite and respectful for most of the very short press conference he held with Andy Burnham, but towards the end he could not resist a jibe about Keir Starmer.
Asked about UK-US relations by a reporter who said they had gone up and down, Trump replied:
No I think they’re up.
Well they’re more up now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.
I think right now, based on my relationship with the prime minister, Andy, I think that, I think we’re doing very well.
At one point the relationship between Trump and Starmer was good. But it got worse as Starmer started to criticise Trump publicly on issues like his proposal to annex Greenland, and his claim British troops avoided frontline action in Afghanistan. And the full rupture came when Keir Starmer refused to allow the US to use British airbases for attacks against Iran at the start of the war.
Trump says Burnham will be 'great PM', and Burnham says they have 'good connection', after friendly first meeting
At the start of the meeting with the press, this is what Donald Trump said about Andy Burnham.
I think he’s going to be a great prime minister. I think he’s got a lot of assets on his side.
We talked about everything from Rolls-Royce to energy, immigration. We covered a lot.
[The UK] is a really special country. And we are with you all the way, Mr Prime Minister.
And Burnham replied:
Thank you Mr President.
That’s wonderful. We really appreciate that.
This relationship matters so much to us. And we will build on that relationship.
You and I have established a good connection in our early discussions, and we’ve taken that further today.
We touched on Ukraine and it’s great to hear what you said today about the potential for progress there.
You know that we’re still ready to play our part in the Middle East in terms of helping you stop the conflict, open the strait [of Hormuz].
Obviously, we’re with you that Iran must never be a nuclear power.
We accepted a call from Saudi Arabia … we are prepared to play our part.
And obviously you were good enough today to let us talk about some issues on trade. The Falklands we mentioned. And you were good enough to listen to us on those issues.
So it has been great to be with you and the team today.
Burnham admits immigration big issue in UK politics
Burnham picks up on the topic of immigration. He says:
It was a very big issue at the Makerfield byelection and a lot of the British media will know that.
And I spoke about it then – our commitment is to get to a controlled approach. That’s what people want to see.
They’re not against migration overall. They know that people work in the NHS and in the care system. [There’s a] difference, though, when it’s managed or when it’s uncontrolled.
And the small boats is a very big issue for people. But crossings this summer were down 50% there or thereabouts on the number six years ago.
So sometimes people don’t hear that the progress is being made. But the progress is being made.
Trump adopts positive tone about Burnham, saying he's 'natural businessperson', after their first meeting
Donald Trump is talking.
He is referring to a “great election win”. It is not clear if he mean’s Labour’s in 2024, or Andy Burnham’s – in Makerfield.
Burnham thanks Trump for his remarks.
He says he thinks they have established a “good connection”.
The BBC’s Chris Mason asks Trump if Burnham is someone he can do business with.
Trump says he thinks he is.
He describes Burnham as a “natural businessperson”.
We’ve had a lot of discussions even before this meeting. We’ve spoken to each other numerous times on the phone. I think so, I think so. He gets it. He understands what he has to do.
(There are not many people who describe Burnham as a natural businessperson. He is a natural communciator, and a natural communicator and leader, but his experience of the business world is pretty limited. Maybe this was just Trump’s way of saying he liked him. Or maybe by “businessperson” he means ‘person you can do a deal with’. Still, it was positive.)
Originally journalists were told they would talk to the press briefly at the start of the meeting.
But now reporters have been told that they will be let in as the meeting ends for some words. Whether that will just be a few platitudes as Trump and Burnham pose for pictures, or whether they will take questions, is not entirely clear.
They are not in the Oval Office in the White House (which is looking even more lavish than usual now that Trump has given it billionaire bling decor). Instead they are at the United Nations building, which is functional and a bit shabby. Here is a shot from the live feed from the room where reporters are waiting.
We were told that the meeting would last for about half an hour, which means it should have been over by now. But nothing ever runs on time at the UN …

articles.title: New US “Fort Trump” military base in Poland “confirmed”, says President Nawrocki
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump”.
Trump himself declared last week that “major progress” was being made towards establishing the base, saying it was thanks to the “bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki”, who is a conservative ally of the US president.
Meanwhile, earlier this week, a Polish deputy defence minister, Stanisław Wziątek, also expressed confidence that the new base would soon be confirmed and said that it could see the number of US troops stationed in Poland rise to around 15,000.
President Karol Nawrocki said he hopes the US will finalize plans to establish a permanent military base in Poland and, if it does, the compound will be christened ‘Fort Trump' https://t.co/SB4DOy5Qp1 pic.twitter.com/aPmvl4JoFO
— Bloomberg TV (@BloombergTV) September 22, 2026
The US military presence in Poland has become a big issue this year following Washington’s unexpected last-minute decision in May to cancel the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 troops.
Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. In June, Poland formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory.
In a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, last week, Trump announced “major progress” in those plans and said that “if this happens, the location [of the base] will be announced very soon”. He called it a “historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance”.
On Tuesday this week, speaking to Bloomberg during a visit to the US for the United Nations General Assembly, Nawrocki confirmed that plans for the base were at an advanced stage.
“The infrastructure is being chosen right now. Consultants from the US have already visited Poland,” he said. “I think that it’s hard for me to give specific dates, but I think that this matter is for sure confirmed because President Trump is famous for keeping his word.”
Nawrocki also expressed confidence that “President Trump will personally be able to participate in the inauguration of Fort Trump”. That name, Fort Trump, was first suggested in 2018 by Nawrocki’s predecessor, Andrzej Duda, when, during Trump’s first term, he sought a permanent US base in Poland.
Poland’s government, which regularly clashes with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and has also at times had tense relations with the Trump administration, has not commented on the idea of naming the new base after the US president.
However, the government is keen for the project to move ahead, and has been doing much of the legwork on making it happen. Although Poland’s president is commander-in-chief of the armed forces, his position is largely ceremonial, and it is the government that is responsible for implementing policy.
On Monday this week, deputy defence minister Stanisław Wziątek told broadcaster RMF that he was “convinced there is full agreement” on establishing the base, with the remaining question being the precise location.
Wziątek said that the announcement could be made before November’s midterm elections in the US, as Trump will be keen to encourage Polish Americans to vote Republican.
💬Kiedy poznamy ostateczną decyzję w sprawie stałej bazy amerykańskiej w Polsce?
💬Jestem przekonany, że pan prezydent @realDonaldTrump będzie chciał zrobić wszystko, aby tak decyzja zachęcająca Polaków do głosowania na Republikanów mogła zapaść przed wyborami – Stanisław… pic.twitter.com/uPWkmdGQod
— RozmowaRMF (@Rozmowa_RMF) September 21, 2026
The deputy defence minister said that the base would be likely to host between 3,000 and 5,000 US troops, with 4,500 the “most realistic estimate, because that is the size of a brigade”.
In total, said Wziątek, Poland hoped to have “around 15,000” US soldiers in Poland, including the roughly 10,000 that have up until now been present on a rotational basis.
The minister admitted that the current rotational presence was lower, around 6,500-7,000, following the cancellation of May’s planned deployment. But he said that the figure should “soon” return to the previous higher level.
When asked about the cost to Poland of establishing the new permanent US base, Wziątek said it would “definitely be more than 15 billion zloty (€3.4 billion) but will depend on the level of involvement of the United States”.
💬Ilu w tej chwili w Polsce jest żołnierzy amerykańskich? Ilu będzie docelowo rotacyjnych żołnierzy i w stałej bazie?
Odpowiada Stanisław Wziątek @MON_GOV_PL w #RozmowaRMF o 7:00 w @Radio_RMF24@RMF24pl @Radio_RMF24 pic.twitter.com/1Zl66upkp8
— RozmowaRMF (@Rozmowa_RMF) September 21, 2026
The US has long been Poland’s most important security partner. In 2023, under President Joe Biden, it established its first permanent military garrison in Poland at Camp Kościuszko in the city of Poznań. The following year, a US missile defence base opened in Redzikowo on Poland’s northern Baltic coast.
This week, the mayor of Poznań, Jacek Jaśkowiak, told newspaper Fakt that his city was one of two locations being considered for the planned new US base. Recent Polish media reports have also identified the provinces of Lower Silesia and West Pomerania as potential locations.
While the Trump administration has chastised many NATO member states for failing to meet the alliance’s defence spending targets, it has hailed Poland, whose defence budget is one of NATO’s highest in relation to GDP, as a “model ally”.
Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery.
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Main image credit: Mikołaj Bujak/KPRP
Daniel Tilles is editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland. He has written on Polish affairs for a wide range of publications, including Foreign Policy, POLITICO Europe, EUobserver and Dziennik Gazeta Prawna.

articles.title: Zelenskyy met with British Prime Minister Burnham and warned of Russia preparing a new massive attack
articles.body:
Zelenskyy met with British Prime Minister Burnham and warned of Russia preparing a new massive attack
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham discussed air defense, winter, energy, and sanctions. Intelligence reported that Russia was preparing an attack.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting with Prime Minister of the United Kingdom Andy Burnham, during which the parties discussed security, strengthening Ukrainian air defenses, preparations for winter, and sanctions pressure on Russia. Following the talks, Zelenskyy said that Ukrainian intelligence had information about Russia preparing a new massive attack, UNN reports.
Details
We discussed in detail with Prime Minister of the United Kingdom Andy Burnham everything related to security, protecting our people, preparations for winter, and the diplomatic opportunities available. I thank the United Kingdom for its continued support for our energy sector. There is a new contribution, and we especially appreciate it as winter approaches
The President noted that Ukraine continues negotiations with its partners to obtain additional air defense systems.
Zelenskyy warned of a new massive attack
There is currently information from intelligence that Russia is preparing a new massive attack against Ukraine
According to him, Ukraine and the United Kingdom also share a common position on the need to maintain sanctions pressure on Russia.
When Ukrainians live under the threat of missile and drone strikes every day, there can be no talk whatsoever of lifting sanctions. The Prime Minister and I have a shared position on this issue: as long as the war continues, sanctions must be maintained and strengthened

articles.title: Sanctions must remain in place and be strengthened as long as war continues, Zelensky says after meeting Burnham
articles.body:
Sanctions must remain in place and be strengthened as long as war continues, Zelensky says after meeting Burnham
Ukrinform reports this, citing the official Facebook page of the President of Ukraine.
“I discussed in detail with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham everything related to security, the protection of our people, preparations for winter, and available diplomatic opportunities. I thank the United Kingdom for its steadfast support for our energy sector. There is a new contribution, and we particularly value it as winter approaches,” the post says.
At the same time, the President added, Ukraine is in constant communication with its partners about finding additional air defense capabilities.
According to him, intelligence currently indicates that Russia is preparing a new massive attack against Ukraine.
“When Ukrainians are living every day under the threat of missile and drone strikes, lifting sanctions is out of the question. The Prime Minister and I see this eye to eye: as long as the war continues, sanctions must remain in place and be strengthened,” Volodymyr Zelensky emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticized the EU’s decision to remove Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

articles.title: Belgium has received 3 more F-35s, bringing the transfer of F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine closer
articles.body:
Belgium has received 3 more F-35s, bringing the transfer of F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine closer
Kyiv • UNN
The number of Belgian F-35As has risen to 7. The country plans to transfer 53 F-16s to Ukraine, with the first of them potentially arriving in 2026.
Another 3 American fifth-generation F-35A fighter jets have arrived in Belgium, with which the country is gradually replacing its F-16s. The decommissioned F-16s are planned to be transferred to Ukraine, Defense Express reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
The new aircraft landed at Florennes Air Base, bringing the number of F-35As based directly in Belgium to 7. A total of 15 such fighter jets have already been manufactured for the country, although 8 remain in the United States for pilot training.
Belgium ordered 34 F-35As back in 2018. The new fleet is planned to achieve full combat readiness in 2030, while the aircraft are expected to be ready to conduct rapid-response operations as early as 2027.
Belgium plans to transfer 53 F-16s to Ukraine
As F-35s are delivered, Belgium will gradually decommission its F-16 fighter jets and transfer them to Ukraine. According to the publication, the first 7 aircraft may arrive as early as 2026.
Overall, Belgium plans to keep the F-16s in service until 2028 and transfer 53 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2029.
The Ukrainian Air Force is already operating F-16s received from other European partners. They are used, in particular, to strike ground targets and intercept Russian missiles and drones.

articles.title: Guterres pleads for 'world built on interdependence' in final General Assembly address
articles.body:
Guterres pleads for 'world built on interdependence' in final General Assembly address
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres pleaded for “a world built on interdependence” Tuesday as he made his final address to the annual gathering of world leaders convening to face a formidable menu of challenges, from climate change and war to inequality and the rise of artificial intelligence.
In a no-nonsense farewell speech, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged global leaders Tuesday to respond to the defining challenge today: Will the world continue on its path to fragmentation, or cooperate to tackle the existential threats from climate crisis, runaway artificial intelligence and intensifying inequalities?
Read more'No peace without justice,' Macron tells UN General Assembly
The UN leader has long implored leaders not to give up on cooperation and shared decision-making in the face of accelerating global challenges and increasing great-powers competition. Tuesday’s message at the UN General Assembly took on additional urgency because he leaves office at the end of this year.
“The fault lines in our world are widening,” he said, citing raging wars, rising temperatures and artificial intelligence, among other matters. Instead of letting the future continue to veer toward fragmentation, transactionalism and mistrust, he called for “a world built on interdependence – and sustained by a dense web of economic, political, social and technological connections”.
His speech opened the main portion of the world's biggest diplomatic meeting of the year. Leaders from the UN's 193 member countries address each other and the international community and air their hopes, plans and grievances.
Guterres also rebuked might-makes-right thinking, telling superpowers to recognise “that their power isn’t so super”. Recent years have made it clear that “military power alone cannot secure peace,” he said.
Yet about an hour after Guterres spoke, US President Donald Trump offered a different and equally frank view of power.
Read moreIran, AI and the ICC: Trump makes threats, touts policies at UN General Assembly
“While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world,” Trump said, touting his country's economic, technological and military footprint.
He reiterated his view that the UN has “great potential” but rebuked it for what he called “imposing the far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats”. He went on to criticise such bodies as the International Criminal Court, to which the US is not a party.
The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will be consumed with wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, DR Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: Can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living?
The future of the United Nations itself will also be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players. Member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful UN Security Council, where the US, Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented.
Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the UN next. Guterres’ second five-year term ends on December 31, and no clear successor has emerged. Guterres closed his speech by acknowledging the forthcoming departure and vowing to “never, ever give up” on the values for which the UN stands.
“Wherever I will be, whatever I will be doing, I will keep championing the conviction that peace is possible,” he said, before leaving the rostrum amid a sustained, standing ovation. He put his hand on his heart.
There is still no question that the UN remains the key gathering place for its member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly, along with dozens of ministers.
Among the headliners Tuesday: Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – whom New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority – will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won’t be coming to the UN because the US refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day.
Read moreUS again denies Palestinian leader visa for UN General Assembly
The United States, under its agreement with the UN to host the organisation, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings.
Equally telling is who else isn’t coming. China’s President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday, yet he is skipping – some diplomats say snubbing – the UN gathering and sending a vice president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn’t coming either, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has backed out.
France's UN ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, said ahead of the gathering that it is “extremely critical” for world leaders to support the UN as the place where the world’s nations meet – especially at a time of such polarisation.
“We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation”.
There is no doubt it’s been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The US failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organisation’s finances in rocky shape.
“While the world still trusts the UN, the global public is eager for change," said former UN deputy secretary-general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member.
The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns.
Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as “a hoax”, and urged continued advances to keep the US ahead of China.
Read moreTrump calls concerns over rogue AI a 'hoax' promoted by a ‘sick conspiracy’
The UN Security Council added a meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue. It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelensky on Wednesday morning.
(FRANCE24 with AP)

articles.title: At least 17 killed in Saudi airstrikes across Yemen: Houthi media
articles.body:
SANAA, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Tuesday that Saudi warplanes carried out 19 airstrikes across three Yemeni provinces over the past 24 hours, while Houthi-run media reported at least 17 killed and 11 wounded in recent strikes.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said in a statement on social media platform X that the strikes targeted the southwestern province of Taiz, the northern province of Al-Jawf, and the northeastern oil-rich province of Marib.
Sarea said Saudi F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets operating from air bases in Khamis Mushait and Taif carried out the attacks, causing deaths and injuries.
He added that the latest attacks brought the Houthi-reported tally of Saudi air and missile attacks since the current escalation began to 936, warning that Saudi Arabia would face "dire" consequences.
The figures could not be independently verified.
Separately, Houthi-run media and officials said the strikes from Monday night through Tuesday had killed at least 17 people and wounded 11 others.
Abdul Qader al-Murtada, head of the Houthis' prisoner affairs committee, said in a statement on X that nine detainees were killed when a Saudi airstrike hit a prison in Al-Hazm, the provincial capital of Al-Jawf, on Monday night.
In another incident in Al-Jawf, Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported that a woman and her child were killed in Saudi airstrikes, with her husband and two other family members wounded.
Earlier Tuesday, al-Masirah reported that three Saudi airstrikes hit a residential house in the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha in Taiz, killing six people, including two children and a woman, and wounding eight others.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia on the Houthi claims.
The strikes came amid an escalating confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, with Saudi airstrikes targeting Houthi-held areas across Yemen and the group launching missiles and drones at targets deep into the kingdom.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 to support the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

articles.title: The Pentagon has unveiled its secret weapon: two idiotic influencers | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.body:
We’re now approaching month seven of a war against Iran that Donald Trump repeatedly assured us would be over in a matter of weeks. Prices are rising, troop morale is plummeting, and there is little evidence things will improve.
The situation is so desperate that the decision makers at the Pentagon have decided to bring out the big guns. I’m not talking about nuclear weapons, although Trump recently threatened to “blow the entire nation [of Iran] up”. No, I’m talking about influencers Jake and Logan Paul, who are famous for doing idiotic stunts on YouTube and getting hit in the face during boxing matches. Last Thursday, Pete Hegseth’s Department of Defense or whatever they’re calling it these days (the Department of War Crimes?) welcomed the Paul brothers to Washington DC “to meet with our warriors” and deliver a motivational speech. In response, former Republican congressman and air force officer Adam Kinzinger wrote, “We aren’t a serious country at the moment.” That about sums it up.
The Paul brothers, to be fair, rose to the occasion as best they could. In a speech which channelled Churchill, if Churchill had suffered several major blows to the head, Logan said that touring the Pentagon had been “a cool experience”. Albeit not quite as cool as being deployed to fight and possibly die in an illegal bombing campaign started by president Trump, a convicted felon, on the advice of Benjamin Netanyahu, an accused war criminal. “I don’t think there is any greater commitment to sacrifice than those who are willing to live, die and fight for their country,” Logan said. Which is why you won’t see him doing it; easier to pocket millions fighting on TV.
As well as giving a pep talk to the military, Jake met up with treasury secretary Scott Bessent and the US treasurer to discuss how “to get more young Americans financially empowered.” That must have been an interesting chat considering how, back in 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission charged the YouTuber with unlawfully promoting crypto assets without disclosing that he was being paid to do so; he eventually settled without admitting or denying the charges. (Logan has also faced a lawsuit linked to a dodgy crypto venture, although the case was eventually dismissed). Exactly the sort of person you want the treasury secretary expending energy talking to when US debt recently topped $40tn for the first time ever and a financial crisis seems to be around the corner.
Just how Jake Paul and Bessent hope to financially empower young Americans is unclear. But it is unlikely to be via the traditional method of working hard at school and then going to university. Jake very much shares the Trump administration’s contempt for education. In 2020 he tweeted that he’s “sick of our education system and how it’s teaching kids 0 real life skills for them to secure there [sic.] own future.” He also once described high school as “kids sitting in Geography to learn where Timbuktu is for no reason.” The reason you learn where Timbuktu is, Jake, is so the US can overthrow it after they’re done with Iran and Greenland.
There has always been a strong vein of anti-intellectualism in US politics. “[T]he subordination of men of ideas to men of emotional power or manipulative skill are hardly innovations of the twentieth century,” Richard Hofstadter wrote in his 1963 book Anti-intellectualism in American Life. “[T]hey are inheritances from American Protestantism.” But while this may not be a new impulse, the Trump administration’s embrace of ignorance is doing damage that can’t be easily undone. The US is stuck in a vicious vacuousness cycle: the Trump administration has slashed research funding and disrupted thousands of grants, leading many promising young academics to flee the US. As expertise is eliminated and critical thinking purged from government institutes, chancers like the Paul brothers are elevated.
Still, I suppose we should count our blessings, before even they are affected by Iran-induced inflation. At least the boneheaded Paul brothers are simply having meetings with high-level Trump administration officials. At least they’re not directly involved with military or economic policy. Although, the way things are going it’s only a matter of time. “I’m going to make a prediction that you will be, in the not-too-distant future, running for political office,” Trump told Jake, who has been a vocal Maga supporter, on stage at a rally earlier this year. “You have my complete and total endorsement.” Could another blond buffoon with zero qualifications become president of the US? Tune in to find out in the next season of America: the Empire Implodes

articles.title: Trump addresses UN General Assembly amid Iran war and tensions with allies – live
articles.body:
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Speaking at the UN general assembly, Donald Trump re-issued his threat to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into Hell” if the regime didn’t capitulate and make a deal.” He also said he was “working closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine” to end the disastrous war, defended his administration’s actions in Latin America – including the midnight raid to arrest former Venezuelan president Nicólas Maduro, defended his drone strikes on boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific, accused Mexico of being effectively controlled by the cartels, and said it was “unacceptable” for the US to share a border with a nation under such conditions, pointed to regime change in Cuba and said he would reject any calls for a “globalist scheme” to control artificial intelligence.
Shortly after his UN address, Trump signed a Greenland deal, which Greenland’s prime minister Jens-Frederick Nielsen said “underlines the importance of the Nato alliance.” In tricky, carefully worded paragraphs, she said the agreement “recognises the US defining historical and ongoing contributions to the security and defence of Greenland,” but it also “respects the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland’s right to self-determination.”
Trump and New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani appeared friendly after a ‘wide-ranging’ meeting at Gracie Mansion. Trump said he hoped Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader.
Trump told a CNN reporter at the UN general assembly on Tuesday that he was “surprised” the outlet was covering him, saying it ‘shouldn’t be here’ after he banned the network alongside Politico and MS Now from the White House on Friday. Answering a reporter’s question following her first appearance of the midterm campaign season, Kamala Harris said, “The man is afraid of the voice of the people and that the people understand and know what he’s doing.”
At a joint press conference on Tuesday, Vice President JD Vance and Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, announced that the federal government was removing 760,000 enrollees from Affordable Care Act insurance marketplaces.
Trump said he is working on a ‘massive’ Belarus, pivoting away from main supplier Canada amid an escalating trade dispute, and moving instead toward an ally of Russia.
Federal immigration officials in Texas prevented US representative Veronica Escobar from fully conducting her congressional oversight duties at a controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center, the lawmaker said in an interview with the Guardian.
Senator John Curtis, a Republican from Utah, published a letter calling for a key Senate committee to investigate Trump’s son over his personal and business dealings with foreign governments, as well as his shady ventures in cryptocurrency and predictions markets. Curtis’ letter follows a bombshell report from ProPublica that found a Russian oligarch with close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, had helped bankroll Trump Jr.’s lavish Bahamas wedding.
The Republican National Committee has sued top election officials in New Jersey, alleging they failed to produce public voter roll records, including the addresses of noncitizen voters.
The Spanish government has decided to allow the Trump administration’s controversial extradition request to extradite wealthy activist James “Fergie” Chambers to continue in the country’s courts.
Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects, is currently imprisoned in Madrid. It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation tied to money Chambers has donated to support Palestinians, including the Sameer Project, in Gaza.
Kamala Harris called Donald Trump’s decision to ban three news organisations from the White House “absolutely abhorrent.”
Answering a reporter’s question following her first appearance of the midterm campaign season, Harris said, “The man is afraid of the voice of the people and that the people understand and know what he’s doing.”
Harris had been speaking at a roundtable on Black maternal health in Michigan alongside Senate-hopeful Abdul El-Sayed.
“He’s trying to stifle the ability of journalists to let the people of America know what’s really going on with their government,” Harris said.
60 Minutes’ blockbuster interview with Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, failed to provide a major ratings boost for the Sunday show, according to audience figures released Tuesday.
Sunday night’s episode of the newsmagazine show drew an average of 6.77m total viewers, the third-smallest audience in the past 25 years for the second episode of a season, adding to a disappointing debut for Bari Weiss, who, as CBS editor-in-chief, rewired the show, firing several high-profile correspondents in the run-up to the new season.
The 59th season debuted on 13 September with an audience down sharply from the 58th season debut, drawing 7.94 million viewers compared with 10 million for last season’s first episode.
Angela Paxton – the Texas state senator who is currently divorcing US Senate-hopeful Ken Paxton – encouraged Republican women to vote the party “even if we’re mad at them,” the Texas Tribune reports.
Paxton said she was divorcing her husband on “biblical grounds,” citing allegations of adultery, in 2025, shortly after her husband announced he would challenge longtime Texas senator John Cornyn. She has not commented on her husband’s race since announcing the divorce, including excluding his name from a list of endorsements in statewide primary races.
According to the Tribune, Angela Paxton addressed a meeting of the Texas Federation of Republican Women on Friday. In a speech titled “The Elephant in the Room” she encouraged the attendees to vote for the party even if they disliked an individual candidate.
“We have more control over that seat and the future when we control the seat — when it’s still in the family, even if we’re mad at them,” she said. “But if we lose it to the other team, the nuances that we want to fix with maybe a certain candidate are nothing compared to what it’s going to take to get it back, right?”
Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer says the shooting of a Venezuelan man by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday “is a direct result of Trump ordering ICE agents to continue deadly traffic stops.”
“ICE must provide a full accounting of what happened, why deadly force was used, and why despite billions in funding agents are still roaming around without cameras and accountability,” Schumer said in a social media post.
After the shooting, Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine.
The supreme court has refused to get involved with a custody dispute between an Alaska surrogate and a California couple whose child was born with a rare and serious heart defect.
On Tuesday, Justice Elena Kagan denied an emergency request from McKenna West, an Alaska nurse and surrogate who had asked the US’s highest court to halt a California court order recognizing the couple, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, as the boy’s legal parents.
In recent weeks, the case has garnered nationwide attention, sparking broader discussions about surrogacy and abortion.
The Cuban delegation withdrew from a session at the UN general assembly after Donald Trump called the country a “failed state”.
“The US government is unable to accept that Cuba is, and has the right to be, a fully independent and sovereign country,” Cuban foreign affairs minister Bruno Rodríguez wrote in a social media post. “The economic blockade, including the energy siege, only threatens Cuba and the rest of the nations. It is an act of genocide and collective punishment. We are a country of peace and we deserve peace.”
As my colleagues Lee Schlenker and Ed Augustin reported last week, “Agrowing cast of Washington and Florida insiders – from billionaire Trump allies and Rubio-linked lobbyists to Cuban exiles – are jockeying for control of the communist-ruled island-nation’s key assets”.
Democratic attorneys general from California and New York have sued the Trump administration over its plans to buy back offshore wind leases as Donald Trump seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels.
California attorney general Rob Bonta said he was suing over removal of a project off his state’s coast planned by Chicago-based Invenergy. The Trump administration said in June it was buying back the company’s US offshore wind leases for four wind projects on the east and west coasts.
New York attorney general Letitia James, meanwhile, led seven states in suits seeking to block the Invenergy deal and another proposal with Bluepoint Wind, which agreed in April to end a wind farm under development off the New York and New Jersey coast.
The deals would hand energy companies $1.4bn in taxpayer dollars in exchange for the cancellation of multiple projects. In all, the Trump administration has pledged nearly $4bn to companies to walk away from projects across the country.
Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Donald Trump, days after María Elvira Salazar called out the US president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants.
Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s US midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump and removed a photograph of the congressman and his wife, Erika, posing with the president, the Miami Herald reported.
Until now, Donalds has proudly touted his close ties with the president, running a Republican primary campaign themed largely on Trump’s endorsement, and displaying a large banner on his website advertising his support.
The move comes as Trump’s overall approval rating fell below 30% for the first time, dragged down by dissatisfaction over his handling of the US economy and the Iran war, and Republicans brace for heavy losses in November, including the possible loss of the party’s majorities in the US House of Representatives and Senate.
Republican National Committee sues New Jersey election officials for refusal to turn over voter records
The Republican National Committee has sued top election officials in New Jersey, alleging they failed to produce public voter roll records, including the addresses of noncitizen voters.
The lawsuit follows New Jersey governor Mikie Sherril’s announcement in July that “a software error” in the state’s motor vehicle registration system added 6,600 noncitizens to the state’s voter registration list beginning in 2023. According to the state, 400 votes were cast by noncitizens – although Donald Trump claimed that “thousands of votes” were cast by noncitizens in the state, in an effort to drum up support for his SAVE America Act.
In 2024, Kamala Harris won New Jersey by more than 252,000 votes – meaning that even if all voters were registered as Democrats, which they were not, their votes would not have swung the presidential election.
In Tuesday’s lawsuit, the RNC states that, New Jersey “objected to or denied” several of its records requests “including the request for records of address confirmation notices”.
In July, assistant attorney general for civil rights Harmeet Dhillon wrote to Sherril requesting the “full names, dates of birth, nationalities, residential addresses, and registration dates and locations” of all 6,600 noncitizen voters.
Sherrill has said she will not provide that information. “We now have certain people that, through no fault of their own, have been registered to vote,” she said at a press conference. “It may imperil their immigration status.”

articles.title: Türkiye follows Ukraine, adapts anti-tank missile against drones
articles.body:
- Roketsan's KARAOK anti-tank missile struck an aerial target for the first time, following a pattern seen in Ukraine of anti-tank missiles adapted against drones.
- The Turkish Army has used KARAOK against ground targets since 2022, and Roketsan has not disclosed further details on the aerial test.
Roketsan, the Türkiye-based missile manufacturer, said its KARAOK anti-tank missile struck an aerial target for the first time, firing the shoulder-launched weapon from a turret mounted on a light tactical vehicle. The company announced the milestone in a Sept. 23 post on X, along with footage showing the missile launching from a turreted mount on a pickup truck and intercepting a target drone built to mimic a Shahed-type one-way attack drone.
KARAOK is a man-portable, fire-and-forget anti-tank guided missile designed to be operated by a single soldier from a shoulder-fired tube. It weighs less than 16 kg (35 pounds) including its launch tube, measures 125 mm in diameter, and uses an imaging infrared seeker to track targets in day or night conditions, with an effective range beyond 2,500 meters. Mounting the missile on a vehicle-based turret lets it be aimed and fired without a soldier holding the launcher, a configuration more common among dedicated air-defense systems than infantry anti-tank weapons. Türkiye’s army has used KARAOK against ground targets since it entered service in 2022.
The test follows a pattern that has become common in Ukraine’s war with Russia, where anti-tank guided missiles built for armor have repeatedly been adapted to hit aerial targets, including the Shahed-type drones Russia has used extensively against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Ukraine’s 1021st Anti-Aircraft Artillery Regiment demonstrated its Stugna-P anti-tank system shooting down a Russian drone on Sept. 13, and Ukrainian forces have separately built an improvised air-defense system called STASH that pairs U.S.-made AGM-114 Hellfire anti-tank missiles with a RADA radar to intercept jet-powered Shahed-type drones traveling too fast for interceptor drones to catch.
That overlap exists because many anti-tank guided missiles already carry the sensors needed to track a moving target and the terminal guidance to steer into it, qualities that work against a drone or slow cruise missile almost as well as against a tank. The U.S. Javelin was designed with some capability against slow, low-flying aircraft from the outset, and Hellfire missiles fired from Apache helicopters have long been used against aerial drones in addition to their primary anti-armor role.
KARAOK has also drawn interest beyond Türkiye. Malaysia signed a contract to become the system’s first foreign buyer, with Roketsan planning to deliver an initial batch of launchers and missiles to the Malaysian Armed Forces in early 2026 to replace the Russian-made Metis-M anti-tank system already in service there. Roketsan has not said whether the turreted, anti-drone configuration shown in this test will become a standard offering or remains experimental.

articles.title: Viral NATO video falsely framed as 'war propaganda' against Russia
articles.body:
Viral NATO video falsely framed as 'war propaganda' against Russia
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
A viral NATO video is being falsely framed online as "war propaganda", with users accusing the Alliance of sharing a "promotional video" designed to prepare the public for imminent war with Russia. But the footage is not new: NATO published it in July 2024 for its 75th anniversary, and it's been stripped of its original context. The claim comes as European leaders warn of growing Russian hybrid threats, including alleged drone, cyber and sabotage activity. Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake.
Moscow is facing growing accusations of targeting NATO countries with its hybrid warfare campaign, as a growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test the Alliance's commitment to supporting Ukraine.
But amid those tensions, a different claim is spreading online: that NATO is preparing the public for an imminent war with Russia.
Pro-Kremlin accounts have been sharing a video they describe as NATO "propaganda" or "promotional material" for a future conflict with Moscow, and some posts have been viewed hundreds of thousands of times, if not millions.
The video was shared by the Russian embassy in the Netherlands, which accused NATO of trying to "inspire the youth to be ready to die for the elites". It was also amplified in the United States by conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, who made further "White genocide" claims about the video's portrayal of diversity.
However the video is not new footage, and it wasn't produced to promote an impending war with Russia. The video was created to celebrate the Alliance's 75th anniversary, and NATO published the video on its official social media accounts in July 2024, ahead of a summit in Washington marking the date.
The footage has since been downloaded, stripped of that context and recirculated online as supposed evidence that NATO is preparing the public for war with Russia.
Whilst the video is being misinterpreted online, this does not mean tensions between NATO countries and Russia are not intensifying.
European leaders have increasingly warned of late about Russian hybrid threats and possible attempts to test NATO's commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said intelligence indicated Russia could be planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on NATO's eastern flank. French President Emmanuel Macron also warned of intensifying Russian hybrid attacks and said he had ordered plans to protect critical infrastructure.
Macron also pointed to a recent drone incident at Germany's Leipzig airport, which German officials attributed to Russia. Other incidents of late have also involved Russian aircraft: NATO jets recently shot down a Russian drone that entered Lithuanian airspace, while a Russian warship was accused of firing flares at a Danish military helicopter.

articles.title: Britain forms squadron to strike threats in orbit
articles.body:
The Royal Air Force is today forming No. III Space Effects Squadron, the first British unit dedicated to disrupting, degrading and denying hostile activity in space, the Ministry of Defence stated.
The squadron is being announced by the Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, at the first UK Space Power Conference today, and will bring together specialist personnel from across the armed forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and defend the satellites the country depends on.
Sir Harv will say: “Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost. No. III Space Effects Squadron will safeguard the vital benefits that space gives to our integrated armed forces, and will be capable of denying those benefits to our adversaries.”
The new unit completes a trio of squadrons, since No. I Space Operations Squadron gives the Royal Air Force the ability to watch what is happening in orbit and No. II Space Warning Squadron provides warning of threats, while according to the department No. III will act against those threats using advanced technology including electronic warfare. It will support both offensive and defensive space operations and is expected to expand as new capabilities enter service.
The department describes the formation as contributing to developing British capabilities for space warfare, including electronic warfare and countermeasures against anti-satellite weapons, and delivering the Control of Space Requirement set out in the UK Space Strategy published earlier this month. That requirement covers maintaining freedom to operate in space while denying adversaries the same freedom.
Britain has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing, the kind that generates long-lived debris fields, and the department says it continues to work through the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space to promote norms and principles of responsible behaviour in orbit. The government describes itself as committed to the peaceful and sustainable use of space while protecting critical infrastructure.
Alongside the announcement, the department restated an £880 million investment between 2026/27 and 2029/30 in space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and in space control activities.
The Strategic Defence Review stated that the ability to operate in, from and through space underpins British security, prosperity and daily life, and the Defence Investment Plan committed to the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability, a trilateral programme with the United States and Australia whose British site is due to begin construction in April 2027 and which will provide continuous radar coverage of geostationary orbit.

articles.title: UK deploys RAF tanker to refuel Saudi jets amid Houthi attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK deploys RAF tanker to refuel Saudi jets amid Houthi attacks
Britain will deploy an RAF tanker to refuel Saudi warplanes amid renewed Houthi attacks on the kingdom, as an escalating battle for strategic territory in Yemen threatens to further destabilise the Red Sea region.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he approved a Saudi request for "defensive air-to-air refuelling", with a single RAF Voyager expected to begin operating from Britain's RAF Akrotiri base in Cyprus in the coming days.
The deployment is expected to last several weeks initially, although Burnham said it would be kept under review.
British officials said the mission would be limited to refuelling Saudi aircraft involved in defending the kingdom against Houthi missile and drone attacks, rather than supporting Saudi strikes inside Yemen.
The move nevertheless expands Britain's military involvement alongside Saudi Arabia at a time when fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces has intensified dramatically.
Earlier this year, the UK deployed its Sky Sabre air defence system to Saudi Arabia to help protect the kingdom against Iranian missile attacks.
Burnham linked the latest deployment to regional stability and Britain's economic interests, saying disruption to major energy routes needed to be prevented as turmoil across the region puts pressure on global energy supplies.
The British deployment comes after the Houthis made sweeping gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast, including the capture of the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Battle for strategic heights
Fighting has since shifted towards the Kahboub Mountains, a range of strategic heights spanning parts of Taiz and Lahj provinces and separating the Red Sea coast from areas of southern Yemen held by forces aligned with the internationally recognised government.
Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters that the Houthis were attempting to seize the heights in an effort to cut off remaining Saudi-backed positions along the Red Sea coast from government-held territory further south.
Control of the mountains could allow the Houthis to consolidate their rapid coastal advances by dominating routes connecting the Red Sea coast with southern Yemen.
Government-aligned forces have meanwhile mounted a counteroffensive aimed at preventing the Houthis from securing the high ground and preserving their ability to push back towards the coast.
The renewed fighting has drawn Saudi Arabia more directly back into the conflict, with Riyadh carrying out air strikes in Yemen while facing repeated Houthi missile and drone attacks on its own territory.
Saudi Arabia has simultaneously sought international assistance to contain the Houthi advance.
US President Donald Trump considered ordering American strikes against the group over the weekend following repeated appeals from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, but ultimately decided to hold off, according to US media reports.
Saudi Arabia has also turned to China, asking Beijing to use its influence with Iran to restrain the Houthis.
China subsequently privately asked Tehran to help rein in the group, Reuters reported last week, citing three Iranian sources familiar with the discussions.
Riyadh's appeals came after the Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast and around Bab al-Mandab heightened concerns over Saudi oil exports and international shipping.
The escalation comes as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the principal route for Gulf oil exports, has already been severely disrupted by the wider conflict involving Iran and the United States.
That has increased the strategic importance of the Red Sea route through Bab al-Mandab, with Burnham saying Britain needed to help keep vital energy routes open.

articles.title: Fake passport images claim Zelenskyy and family chose Israel as homeland
articles.body:
A photo amassing thousands of views on social media allegedly shows a scan of Zelenskyy's passport, with Israel as his homeland. Not only are the allegations false, but they've been doing the rounds since 2023.
A fake photo circulating online of two alleged Israeli passports belonging to Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, allegedly shows that the Ukrainian president and his family have chosen Israel as their homeland instead of Ukraine.
The Facebook post was published at the beginning of September alongside the caption: "You can twist it any way you like, but we always come back to the same point: Zelenskyy and his family have a homeland of choice that inspires, protects and supports him in everything he does, and that homeland is certainly not Ukraine. This is common knowledge, just as it is common knowledge who his backers are at the top of the Ukrainian establishment, but people prefer to turn a blind eye so as not to disturb those pulling the strings. Shalom."
There is no truth behind these claims. The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, contacted Ukrainian official sources who denied them.
Furthermore, Ukrainian public officials are not permitted to hold multiple citizenships, unlike members of the general public, under a recent law which officially came into effect in January of this year.
Additionally, the false passport belonging to Zelenska lists the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic as her place of birth. This is inaccurate, as official identity documents issued for individuals born in Ukraine before independence routinely list Ukraine rather than the defunct Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, which was one of the constituent republics of the Soviet Union from 1922 until 1991.
The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, also ran it through the image detector Hive Moderation, which revealed it to be AI-generated.
The fake passport appears to have been created based on a sample template published on the Council of Europe website.
Fake Zelenskyy passports resurfaced
It's not the first time false passports attributed to Zelenskyy and Zelenska have circulated online.
In April 2026, an image of an alleged Israeli passport of Zelenskyy was shared on Instagram, X and Facebook, gathering thousands of views, likes and reshares.
These posts claimed that the Ukrainian president was an agent for Israel's intelligence agency, whose main mission was "to Ukrainianise Europe and lead it to its own self-destruction".
In addition to a significant portion of the passport being cropped in the image, there is a spelling error in Zelenskyy's name.
According to the president's official website, his last name is stylised as "Zelenskyy" in English, not "Zelensky", as the alleged passport shows.
In fact, stories about Zelenskyy and Zelenska's alleged passport have been doing the rounds since at least 2023.
For instance, a photo of the first lady was shared on pro-Russian channels and in several Facebook posts.
In one of these posts, the caption can read: "While Ukrainian President Zelensky travels the world begging for money and weapons for his war, his wife spent a lovely vacation in Israel and even obtained an Israeli passport. Interestingly, is Mrs Zelensky preparing for a possible escape from Ukraine?"
All of these posts follow the same playbook: use an AI-generated passport to invent a scandal with some real elements to target Ukraine and undermine support from its allies, as Russia's war against the country continues.
These techniques are common tactics used among pro-Russian networks in their disinformation campaigns.
The posts about the alleged Israeli passports stand at odds with one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's supposed justifications for his full-scale invasion: when it began in February 2022, Putin pledged to oversee the "demilitarisation and de-Nazification" of Ukraine.
However, as the grandson of a Holocaust survivor, Zelenskyy has Jewish origins and has previously addressed the series of attacks on his religious background by the Kremlin.
"How can I be a Nazi?" Zelenskyy said in 2022, just before the full-scale invasion, in a video address directed at the Russian people in the Russian language. "Explain it to my grandfather, who went through the entire war in the infantry of the Soviet army, and died a colonel in an independent Ukraine."
