articles.title: Britain prepares for war in space as threats grow
articles.body:
Britain is developing capabilities for what it explicitly describes as “orbital warfare”, including systems able to disrupt, degrade and deny hostile activity in space as the Armed Forces prepare for conflict extending beyond the Earth’s atmosphere.
Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, Chief of the Air Staff and professional head of the Royal Air Force, set out the direction of travel at the UK Space Power Conference in London, warning that adversaries are not waiting for Britain to complete its preparations.
The conference is delivered by UK Space Command and led in partnership with the Freeman Air & Space Institute. Its programme brings together senior figures from Defence, government, the UK Space Agency and allied military organisations.
Smyth said: “Space has never been more important for our nation’s defence and security, for our prosperity and our daily lives, and our adversaries are not waiting until we’re ready for them.”
He added: “We must now get on with delivery of space capability and operational effect at pace.”
The most direct indication of how far that effort is moving came when Smyth described the development of capabilities specifically intended for operations against hostile activity in orbit.
He said: “To help our nation fulfil the control of space requirement, UK Defence is now developing capabilities for orbital warfare.”
Smyth defined this as “actions and effects conducted within space to achieve military objectives”, alongside electronic warfare, systems intended to counter anti-satellite weapons and other supporting operations.
He said: “These capabilities will help us to deter threats, defend our critical space infrastructure, and reduce an adversary’s freedom to operate against the UK and against our allies.”
The language marks a shift from treating space primarily as a supporting domain for communications, navigation and surveillance towards preparing to contest it directly if necessary.
Smyth said the objective was to secure freedom of action for Britain and NATO while denying an adversary the same advantage.
He said: “Through a whole-of-government approach, the UK will safeguard allied space interests. We will gain and maintain our freedom to operate in space, and we will deny our adversaries that same freedom.”
That effort is being backed by several large investment lines. Smyth said £2.3 billion is being committed to satellite communications between now and 2030, alongside £880 million for space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and space control, and £440 million for novel space technology.
Skynet remains central to the military communications architecture. Smyth described the satellite system as the backbone of Britain’s sovereign global communications capability and said an additional £50 million had been allocated to extend the life of the existing Skynet 5 satellites.
Skynet 6A is due to join them next year, while allied and commercial satellite communications are also expected to provide additional capacity and resilience.
Britain is also expanding its ability to detect and understand activity in orbit. Smyth pointed to RAF Fylingdales, the planned Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability being developed with Australia and the United States, and a growing network of optical and commercial sensors feeding the National Space Operations Centre.
He said the Borealis command, control and data-processing system had reached initial operating capability six months ahead of schedule under a five-year, £65 million programme, giving commanders a better picture of activity in space.
The UK is also examining newer sensor technologies, including neuromorphic systems intended to search large areas of space for unexpected activity around satellites while using considerably less power and communications bandwidth.
Those surveillance systems are intended to support the wider military effort rather than operate in isolation. Smyth described space as the “connective tissue” of the integrated force, linking communications, surveillance and targeting systems across land, sea and air.
Space-based intelligence is also expected to feed the Digital Targeting Web, a £1.8 billion programme intended to connect sensors, commanders and weapons and reduce the time between detecting a target and acting against it.
Alongside the new technology, Defence is expanding the military organisation responsible for operating it. No. 1 Space Operations Squadron already supports activity through the National Space Operations Centre, while No. 2 Space Warning Squadron carries out operations associated with RAF Fylingdales.
A new No. 3 Space Effects Squadron will provide personnel specifically for offensive and defensive space operations, with Smyth saying it will “disrupt, degrade, and deny hostile activity to defend UK space interests and gain operational advantage for the integrated force.”
Plans are also being developed for further numbered squadrons covering areas including tactics and training, the deep-space radar programme and space defence as part of a wider integrated air, space and missile defence structure.
Smyth was careful to frame the build-up as deterrence rather than an intention to initiate conflict.
He said: “No one wants a war in space. We are positioning to deter this. The UK will always operate responsibly in ways that promote stability and avoid escalation.”
But he also made clear that Defence is preparing for the possibility that deterrence fails.
He concluded that Britain must be able to “monitor space, make effective decisions, deter our adversaries, and, if necessary, prevail in this vital yet increasingly contested domain.”

articles.title: 3 killed, over 40 injured as Russia, Ukraine trade accusations about overnight airstrikes
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
- Ukraine claims it shot down 122 drones launched by Moscow overnight
 
At least three people were killed and over 40 others were injured in Russia and Ukraine as both countries continued to trade accusations concerning overnight airstrikes on Wednesday.
 
In Ukraine, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) said on Telegram that a warehouse, a fuel station, and an office building in the Holosiivskyi district and another fuel station in the Darnytskyi district were damaged in an overnight attack on the country’s capital, during which drone debris also fell at a location in the Solomianskyi district.
 
“As of 10 am (0700GMT), one person has died and seven others have been injured following a hostile attack on the capital,” it said.
 
*The KMVA later said that the number of those killed in the Ukrainian capital had risen to two, while 23 others were injured.
 
Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said that one person was killed after Russian strikes targeted port and civilian infrastructure in the southern region, including an Antigua and Barbuda-flagged commercial cargo vessel and an unspecified number of warehouses.
 
“Due to numerous Russian attacks, rescuers from the Mykolaiv region have joined in the efforts to extinguish the fires,” Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said, commenting on strikes in the Odesa region.
 
The DSNS also reported that 12 others were injured due to strikes in the country’s Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Zhytomyr regions.
 
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that the country’s air defenses shot down 122 Russian drones overnight.
 
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed hitting a storage facility and an industrial enterprise in Kyiv and its surrounding region that are allegedly involved in the production of drones and drone components.
 
It also claimed striking three logistics centers in Odesa used to supply Ukraine’s military, a drone warehouse in the Odesa region, and a vessel “while it was delivering military cargo to the port of Odesa.”
 
Earlier, the ministry further claimed that it shot down 514 drones launched by Ukraine overnight over 18 regions, as well as the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.
 
Alexander Shuvaev, acting governor of Russia’s border region of Belgorod, said in a statement that eight people were wounded in five districts due to Ukrainian strikes over the past day, with two of them in serious condition.
 
In the border region of Bryansk, acting governor Yegor Kovalchuk said two people were injured due to Ukrainian drone strikes in the villages of Kryukov and Churovichi.
 
Ukrainian authorities have not yet commented on strikes in Russia.
 
Both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
 
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: Zelensky calls for pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil
articles.body:
Zelensky calls for pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil
Vladimir Zelensky has attempted to blame New Delhi over the West’s failure to end the conflict in Ukraine, right after the Indian foreign minister discussed peace efforts and bilateral cooperation with his Ukrainian counterpart in New York.
”Russia is basing its economy on India, sometimes Turkey and China,” Zelensky said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal on Tuesday.
The Ukrainian leader is in New York seeking more weapons and cash amid a $27 billion hole in Ukraine’s budget and a frontline collapse. The conflict is now in its fifth year, laying bare the West’s foreign policy failures, and Zelensky seemed to be making a case to US President Donald Trump to use his new sanctions authority to punish Russia’s trading partners.
But in India, the largest buyer of Russian oil besides China, the pitch has come across more as a call to punish New Delhi specifically.
Trump, who is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping soon in New York, would be loath to sanction China, especially after Beijing retaliated against earlier US tariffs with restrictions on exports of rare-earth metals and magnets that are crucial to US industries.
“Russia is basing its economy on India” and “ sometimes Turkey and China”. 
How can he make this ridiculous assertion?
China is by far Russia’s biggest trade partner, including in energy.
Turkey is very critical as a country for Russia. Russia and Turkey are connected by major… https://t.co/Jr7IsZzcOS
Russian oil accounted for about 45% of New Delhi’s crude imports in August, at around 2.1 million barrels per day. The numbers were slightly lower in September, tracking at about 1.9 million barrels per day, according to commodity analytics firm Kpler.
India has said it remains committed to securing energy supplies for its 1.4 billion people and will take the necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests amid repeated US tariff threats. New Delhi has also warned Washington of the sanctions impacting bilateral ties and global energy markets.
”This conflict … will not be solved because somebody is buying or not buying oil or alumina or minerals or metals or fertilizer,” Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar had said earlier this month in Kiev. He had discussed peace efforts, bilateral cooperation, and developments in the Black Sea, affecting markets with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha in New York just before Zelensky gave his interview.
Moscow’s oil revenue has increased amid the disruptions in the Middle East caused by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, but its non-energy trade with the Global South has also expanded.
Russia remains an important source of minerals and metals throughout the world amid supply chain disruptions. The US, too, has carved out exemptions for Russian uranium in the sanctions law it just passed.
Zelensky’s interview triggered some anger in Indian foreign policy circles. “How can he make this ridiculous assertion?” former Indian foreign secretary Kanwal Sybal posted on X. “China is by far Russia’s biggest trade partner, including in energy. Zelensky is targeting us openly.”

articles.title: Lukashenko will gladly let Putin use Belarus to attack Ukraine – Belarusian opposition leader
articles.body:
Lukashenko will gladly let Putin use Belarus to attack Ukraine – Belarusian opposition leader
Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya has warned of a real threat of increased Russian provocations against Ukraine from Belarusian territory.
Source: Tsikhanouskaya on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, as quoted by Ukrinform
Quote: "Of course, this is a real possibility. If Russia at some point again wants to attack Ukraine in any way from the northern border, then [self-proclaimed Belarusian President Alexander] Lukashenko will be very happy to provide territory, logistics, and Belarusian infrastructure to help [Russian leader Vladimir] Putin achieve his goals and intentions."
Details: Tsikhanouskaya said that hopes that Lukashenko can be distanced from Putin are futile.
"It is impossible because they have this special symbiotic friendship; they use each other, and they need each other," she explained.
She also pointed out that Belarusian infrastructure – "logistics and antennas for directing drones – is already being used, and at any moment, if the Kremlin needs it, Belarusian capabilities will be used".
According to Tsikhanouskaya, repeaters are being installed not only along the border with Ukraine but also along the border with European Union countries.
Quote: "So, the escalation or provocation may not only be against Ukraine but also against European countries. And, of course, we need to closely monitor what is happening in Belarus."
Details: Asked whether Lukashenko was acting out of fear of Putin, she answered in the affirmative, while stressing that this in no way justifies his policies.
Quote: "He has allowed Russia to penetrate our Belarusian system – the media, education, economy, and defence industry – meaning that he is allowing Russia to quietly occupy Belarus. Russification is being carried out intensively in our country – all of this with Lukashenko's consent."
Details: Tsikhanouskaya believes that Lukashenko is not interested in Ukraine's victory because Russia is his main ally and supports him economically and politically.
"He would, of course, like Russia to win," she stressed.
Lukashenko, in her view, "understands that Ukraine's victory would be a catastrophe for him personally, because a weakened Putin would mean less support for the regime in Belarus".
She also noted that Lukashenko benefits from the war, "making money from the blood of Ukrainians". She noted that 500-600 Belarusian companies produce optics and microchips, purchase various components for Russia's military machine while bypassing sanctions and supply Russia with petroleum products. In addition, the Belarusian regime is also building warehouses for Russia's largest online retailer Wildberries.
Background: At the beginning of September, Tsikhanouskaya said that Russia could use Belarusian territory and military infrastructure for provocations against NATO countries and further escalation of tensions.

articles.title: Taiwan to maintain 'close contact' with US on arms sales ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
articles.body:
Taiwan will continue to keep in close touch with the US to promote the implementation of arms sales according to plan, a defense ministry official said on Wednesday, ahead of a meeting between the US and Chinese leaders in Washington.
China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has repeatedly demanded US arms sales end.
While US President Donald Trump approved an $11 billion package for Taiwan in December, the largest ever, he said in May after visiting Beijing that a second package, worth some $14 billion, was being kept in abeyance.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to press Trump to halt sales when the two of them meet in Washington this week.
Speaking to reporters in southern Taiwan's Tainan during a media trip, Taiwan defense ministry deputy spokesperson Chiao Fu-chun said maintaining security and stability in the Indo-Pacific region was a "common interest of democratic nations."
"The US government and Congress have repeatedly expressed their support for Taiwan's ability to defend itself," he added.
"Therefore, we will continue to maintain close contact with the US Department of War and continue to promote the implementation of arms sales according to plan."
Taiwan's domestic weapons development
Taiwan President Lai Ching-te has embraced Trump's call for US allies to spend more on their defense.
While the US is Taiwan's most important arms supplier, Taipei has its own weapons development program, covering everything from submarines and fighter jets to long-range missiles.
Taiwan's army on Wednesday showed off its new eight-wheeled armored combat vehicle fitted with a 105mm gun, practicing live-fire exercises to demonstrate the domestically made weapon's fighting abilities.
The military also put on display, but did not fire, some of its US-made weapons, such as Lockheed Martin-made HIMARS rockets.
Taiwan routinely holds live-fire drills and takes reporters to military bases to watch exercises.
China has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, and its military operates around the island on an almost daily basis.
Taiwan's government rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, saying only the Taiwanese people can decide their future.

Ukraine Secures €90 Billion Loan Support in High-Level EU Financial Talks
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held talks with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to secure Ukraine's financial stability through 2026 and 2027, as reported by NV on September 22.
During the discussion, President Zelenskyy expressed gratitude for the European Union's decision to provide a €90 billion ($106 billion) loan.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He emphasized that Ukraine is fulfilling all required commitments to reduce its budget deficit, while both parties agreed to develop additional financial support mechanisms.
The two leaders also focused on economic sanctions against Russia. President Zelenskyy described any proposals to lift sanctions on Russian oligarchs as "suicidal and counterproductive," stressing that the war ends through strength rather than concessions to those close to the aggressor.
He thanked von der Leyen for her willingness to add more Russian individuals to the EU sanctions list, stating that "it is precisely such steps that bring about a worthy peace and guaranteed security."
On September 11, 2026, the European Union approved $7.1 billion for Ukraine to spend on air defense, drones, and missiles under the Ukraine Support Loan, as announced by EU Commissioner Andrius Kubilius.
The decision was reported by a correspondent for the Ukrainian outlet Babel on September 11. The approval also cleared the way for Ukraine to purchase American PAC-3 missiles for its Patriot systems.
Previously, EU envoys agreed to remove billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the Russian sanctions list while extending restrictions for around 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years.
The decision was reached after Latvia lifted its veto and abstained from the vote, following reports that France and Luxembourg had pushed for the exclusions.

articles.title: Wife of US seismologist detained in China says Trump will ask Xi to free him
articles.body:
The wife of a US expert on North Korean nuclear tests who has been imprisoned in China since late 2024 said on Tuesday the White House has assured her that US President Donald Trump will ask Chinese leader Xi Jinping to free her husband when the pair meet this week.
Yufang Rong said she feared that Beijing planned to try her Chinese-born husband, Youlin Chen, on fabricated espionage charges even though his US-funded research was openly published, used publicly available data and was done in collaboration with Chinese scientists.
Trump will welcome Xi on Wednesday for their second meeting since May as the heads of the world's leading powers seek stability amid tensions ranging from trade to Iran and Taiwan.
Rong said she was assured during a Tuesday meeting at the White House with officials from the State Department and National Security Council that Trump would ask Xi to free her husband.
Chen, 54, is one of two Americans held by Beijing that the US has designated as "wrongfully detained," making their release a top priority. The other is Min Zin, a scholar arrested in June.
Rong said she was told that Trump also would press Xi to release Min Zin.
Trump raised Chen's case with Xi during a visit to Beijing in May, but it produced no action, Rong said.
"Resolving the wrongful detentions of US citizens is always a top priority for the president," a senior US official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said that the "relevant US person" is suspected of engaging in activities that endanger China's national security and violate Chinese law.
"China is a country with rule of law, and there is no such thing as wrongful detention," spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing, without elaborating and referring to Chen.
Chen's research funded by US Air Force, State Department
Chen, whose detention was revealed by Reuters in July, is a seismologist with a US government contractor. His work detecting shockwaves from North Korean underground nuclear tests has been openly funded by the State Department and the US Air Force Research Laboratory.
He became a US citizen in 2011 and settled in the Boston area.
He was arrested by Chinese state security officers on November 5, 2024, at Beijing International Airport as he prepared to fly home after visiting family and lecturing at two universities. Rong said her husband had been interrogated more than 100 times.
"I can't imagine how hard his life is there every day," she said.
She believes that China wants to use her husband's expertise to improve its ability to conceal nuclear tests using decoupling, a technique in which a device is detonated inside a large underground chamber to reduce the size of the shockwaves.
The US has accused China of using decoupling to try to mask a low-yield nuclear test blast on June 22, 2020. China, which, like the US, has signed but not ratified a 1996 international ban on nuclear tests, denies conducting the test.
US officials obly allowed to visit Chen once a month
US embassy officials had been allowed to visit Chen for about 30 minutes once a month, always in the presence of Chinese officials, Rong said. They read out letters she had written to him, and he dictated his replies.
"They record his appearance, his mental status, and just anything that they observe," she recounted, adding that Chen's Chinese lawyer was not allowed to discuss his visits with her.
Rong is concerned about the conditions of her husband's confinement, where she said he received substandard medical care and food. He suffered from high blood pressure and diabetes.
Asked what she would say to her husband if she could see him, Rong replied: "'Be strong. Be optimistic. There are a lot of people helping you. You will come back for sure.'"

articles.title: Zelenskyy summed up what he managed to discuss with Trump and what the next steps will be to end the war with the Russian Federation

Zelenskyy summed up what he managed to discuss with Trump and what the next steps will be to end the war with the Russian Federation

Ukraine proposed an energy truce and called for China to be involved in pressuring Russia. Zelenskyy is also asking for Patriot missiles and a trilateral meeting.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke about the results of the talks with U.S. President Donald Trump and the next steps that could help end the war with the russian federation. These include an energy ceasefire, involving China in diplomatic efforts, strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, and a possible trilateral meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States, and the russian federation, reports UNN.
Details
President Trump, our teams, and I discussed how to end the war. This is a priority. We are ready. I am not sure whether russia is ready today, but in any case, we discussed an energy ceasefire
The President emphasized that Ukraine is ready for such a ceasefire provided that russian strikes on energy infrastructure, power grids, heating systems, and water-supply systems cease. According to him, the American side should convey this proposal to the russian federation.
Zelenskyy asked Trump to involve China
A separate topic was Trump’s upcoming meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Zelenskyy urged the U.S. president to use Beijing’s influence over russia.
I told the President very frankly that we believe that if he also involves President Xi, he has influence over Putin. If we want to end this war not only in words, then we all must work on it around the clock—for the sake of the people
The presidents also discussed Ukraine’s preparations for winter. Kyiv asked Washington to provide a winter package of missiles for Patriot systems and licenses to produce such missiles. Zelenskyy also emphasized the need for security guarantees for Ukraine.
In the Ukrainian president’s view, one of the key next steps could be a trilateral meeting of the leaders.
In my opinion, the most important step President Trump can take is to organize a trilateral meeting at which the leaders will be able to raise all sensitive issues and try to end the war

articles.title: Russia Is Dropping More Glide Bombs on Ukraine Per Day Than US Did During Iran Air Campaign
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Is Dropping More Glide Bombs on Ukraine Per Day Than US Did During Iran Air Campaign
Russian forces dropped 8,766 guided aerial bombs on Ukraine in August 2026, bringing the daily rate of their use above that recorded for guided bomb strikes during the recent US air campaign against Iran.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 22, Russia used an average of 283 aerial bombs equipped with Universal Gliding and Correction Modules, known as UMPK, per day during August. The outlet based its comparison with US operations on Pentagon data and research by the Royal United Services Institute.
During the US-led Operation Epic Fury against Iran, American aircraft employed an estimated 211 to 237 guided aerial bombs per day, according to Militarnyi’s calculations.
The comparison concerns the rate at which guided aerial munitions were released rather than the overall scale, capabilities, targets, or operational conditions of the respective air campaigns.
Russia’s current rate remains below that recorded during the main phase of the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003. Militarnyi estimated that US and coalition aircraft used roughly 509 precision-guided munitions per day during that period.
The 2003 Iraq campaign involved extensive use of precision-guided weapons. US Air Force data shows that 19,948 of the 29,199 munitions employed during the initial campaign were guided weapons.
Russia’s UMPK kits and the US-developed Joint Direct Attack Munition, or JDAM, are based on a broadly similar approach: adding guidance and control systems to existing stocks of conventional free-fall bombs rather than producing an entirely new weapon.
The US Air Force describes JDAM as a guidance kit that converts conventional unguided bombs into precision weapons using inertial navigation and GPS guidance.
Russia has pursued the same general concept with UMPK-equipped bombs, allowing aircraft to release modified conventional bombs from greater distances. RUSI reported in February 2025 that Russia had ordered more than 70,000 UMPK glide-bomb kits for that year alone as production expanded during the full-scale war.
The August figure illustrates the continuing expansion of Russia’s use of glide bombs against Ukraine. During the final ten days of July, Russian forces also struck Pavlohrad, around 75 kilometers from the front line, three times with guided aerial bombs, according to Militarnyi.
The outlet said the attacks could indicate renewed use of the jet-powered UMPB-5R extended-range bomb.
Russia has also expanded production of other relatively low-cost precision weapons. In September, The Wall Street Journal reported that Russia was rapidly moving new jet-powered systems, including the Geran-5 drone and Banderol cruise missile, from battlefield testing into serial production, with both weapons estimated to cost around $100,000 each.

articles.title: SSU detains Russian strike spotter on Sloviansk front
articles.body:
SSU detains Russian strike spotter on Sloviansk front
According to Ukrinform, the SSU reported this.
The investigation established that the spotter was a resident of a frontline settlement who had been recruited by Russian forces and was evading mobilization.
The Russian intelligence service took notice of him because of anti-Ukrainian comments he posted in chats on Telegram channels, while rarely leaving his home.
After being recruited, the suspect began discreetly questioning his wife about locations where Ukrainian troops were concentrated, which she might have seen while staying in Sloviansk and nearby areas.
He stored the information he gathered on his smartphone as approximate markers on Google Maps for subsequent reporting to his Russian handlers.
It was established that the agent was in contact with the Russian GRU through a liaison officer from the Joint Strategic Command of the Moscow Military District.
They used a popular messaging app with anonymous accounts to communicate.
SSU officers exposed the agent at an early stage of his work for the GRU, documented his espionage activities and detained him at his place of residence.
The suspect’s mobile phone and tablet containing evidence of his cooperation with the enemy were seized.
SSU investigators notified him that he was suspected under Part 2 of Article 111 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code – high treason committed under martial law.
The suspect is being held in custody without the right to bail. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Security Service of Ukraine recently exposed an electrician who had been directing Russian strikes against facilities in Dnipro.
Photo: SSU

articles.title: Explosions, smoke reported near oil refinery in Russia's Bashkortostan
articles.body:
Drones reportedly struck an area near an oil refinery in the city of Ufa, the capital of Russia's Republic of Bashkortostan, on Sept. 23, Russian independent outlet Astra reported, citing local residents.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed 514 drones overnight over 18 regions, including Bashkortostan, occupied Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
Local residents reported hearing explosions in Ufa, while local Telegram channels said air defenses were operating over the city, according to Astra.
Astra's OSINT analyst suggested that smoke rose in the area of the Ufa oil refinery, although the analyst said it could also have originated from a nearby thermal power plant.
A "drone threat" alert was also issued in Bashkortostan, while temporary restrictions were imposed on arrivals and departures at Ufa airport, according to Rosaviatsiya.
The Kyiv Independent cannot independently verify the accuracy of the report. Russian authorities had not commented on a drone attack on the region as of publication, and the Ukrainian military hadn't confirmed the strike.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have emerged as one of the most economically significant aspects of Kyiv's long-range drone strategy, contributing to nationwide fuel shortages and sharply reducing refinery output over the summer.
Half of Russia's six largest diesel-producing refineries have cut or completely halted output in September following Ukrainian drone attacks.
As Ukraine continues to target Russian energy facilities, U.S. President Donald Trump has called for Kyiv to halt its strikes on oil refineries, claiming the attacks were contributing to a global diesel shortage as his war against Iran disrupts fuel supplies worldwide.
"Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump said on Sept. 13. "Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he's causing a shortage of diesel."

articles.title: Iraq extends armed groups disarmament deadline to June 2027
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraq extends armed groups disarmament deadline to June 2027
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi has agreed with leaders of the country's powerful pro-Iran political bloc to give armed groups until June 2027 to complete their disarmament, sources in Baghdad told The New Arab, extending a process initially expected to conclude by the end of September.
The agreement was reached with leaders of Iraq's pro-Iran Coordination Framework, which holds the largest bloc in parliament, before Al-Zaidi travelled to the United States for the UN General Assembly and talks with US officials, the sources said.
The move effectively gives powerful armed factions another nine months to bring their weapons under state control, amid continued resistance from some groups and disagreements over how the process should be implemented.
Al-Zaidi had previously committed to bringing weapons outside state control under government authority by 30 September, following attacks by pro-Iran armed groups on US bases during the war on Iran and subsequent US air strikes on their positions.
Under the new plan, the process would instead be completed by 30 June 2027, with the implementation phase expected to begin in January.
By extending the timeframe, Al-Zaidi hopes to remove the remaining justifications cited by armed factions that have refused to surrender their weapons or fully integrate into Iraq's state security forces.
A new directorate will reportedly be established within the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) to oversee the process, operating under the supervision of the Iraqi government.
The body would be responsible for receiving and cataloguing weapons, ammunition and military equipment held by armed groups, identifying where they are stored and establishing procedures governing their use.
However, the weapons would remain within facilities overseen by the PMF rather than being handed directly to the Iraqi government, a provision that could become a key point of contention with Washington.
Members and leaders of armed factions would also receive immunity from prosecution and retain the right to participate in Iraq's political process if they sign pledges to refrain from armed activity outside state authority.
Disagreement over who controls the weapons
A key dispute remains over who will ultimately control the groups' arsenals.
Washington has pushed for the Iraqi state to establish a monopoly over weapons, while the proposed arrangement would leave the PMF playing a central role in overseeing arms surrendered by the factions.
The US reportedly considers transferring weapons from faction-controlled warehouses to storage facilities that remain under PMF authority insufficient to meet its demands for weapons to be brought fully under state control.
Baghdad, however, faces considerable obstacles in forcing the issue.
Several powerful armed groups continue to resist full disarmament, while the Iraqi government has sought to avoid a military confrontation with factions that retain significant military and political influence.
Pro-Iran groups have also set a series of conditions for giving up their weapons, including the full withdrawal of US forces from Iraq and Turkish troops from northern Iraq, the restoration of what they describe as Iraq's full sovereignty over its territory, stronger Iraqi air defences and federal control over the borders of the autonomous Kurdistan region.
The dispute has complicated Al-Zaidi's attempt to fulfil his pledge to bring all weapons under state authority while avoiding a confrontation with groups that form part of the country's broader political and security establishment.
'Very difficult, indeed impossible'
Uday al-Khadran, a member of the Coordination Framework, told The New Arab that resolving the issue by the end of September had become "very difficult, indeed impossible", citing resistance among armed groups and the absence of mechanisms capable of implementing the process.
He nevertheless said the factions would eventually comply with the government's demands.
"Everyone will ultimately hand over the weapons," al-Khadran said. "But the matter requires arrangements, understandings and sufficient time to complete the process."
He added that negotiations were continuing and that the parties had yet to reach a final agreement on all aspects of the plan.
The priority, al-Khadran said, was to reach an arrangement acceptable to the parties involved that would ultimately bring weapons under state control.

articles.title: Witkoff, Kushner meet mediators as Iran sets demands for reopening Hormuz
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with mediators to discuss a possible deal to end the Iran conflict.
Trump told reporters at the United Nations that US officials had had a "very good" three-hour meeting on Tuesday with the Iranian delegation.
He said that Washington and Tehran were moving toward a settlement, while a senior Iranian official said Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the US eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.
"We are completely isolating Iran financially and simply applying pressure, because we hope they will do the right thing quickly-before it’s too late," Trump said. "You know, there will come a point when it’s too late, and we will no longer have the option of allowing them to survive as a nation."
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in a meeting during which Iran's conditions to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz were conveyed to the US, according to Iran's state media.
Iran sets Hormuz reopening conditions amid renewed US talks
Conditions for reopening the strait include immediate lifting of the naval blockade, immediate release of frozen Iranian assets and end of war across all 'resistance' fronts, state media added.
Trump's remarks came just hours after he repeated a threat at the UN General Assembly to annihilate Iran if it failed to strike a deal.
Speaking after a meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations in New York, Trump said: "They want to talk to us. They have been talking to us; even today they've been talking to us, and the relationship is developing.
"But we can't let them - and they understand that - we can't let them have a nuclear weapon."
Trump meets with Middle East partners
US President Donald Trump also met with Middle Eastern leaders on the sidelines of the UN to discuss bringing an end to the war in Gaza and addressing tensions with Iran.
During the meeting, Trump commended the US and its partners' efforts in the region and praised the participating nations for their regional cooperation, crediting them with successfully delivering humanitarian aid to Gaza and securing the release of hostages held there.
Trump said the nations represented at the meeting "invested billions of dollars in helping Gaza - in helping the people."
"The people around this table made that possible," he added.
Referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Trump stated that he's a "tough cookie, don't mess around with him, he's tough, he's a fantastic guy."
Trump also warned Iran in his speech to "do the right thing fast before it's too late."

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones, including "Banderols" - how the air defense performed
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones, including "Banderols" - how the air defense performed
Kyiv • UNN
During the night of September 23, Russia launched 161 drones at Ukraine, including 82 jet-powered Shaheds. Air defense shot down or suppressed 122 targets.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones during the night of September 23; 122 of them were shot down or suppressed, including three "Banderols." UNN reports this, citing data from the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force.
What Russia used to strike and where from
According to the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force, during the night of September 23 (starting at 18:00 on September 22), the enemy attacked with 161 Shahed-type attack UAVs (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, Parodiya-type decoy drones, as well as "Banderol"/"Dan-T" drones, launched from the following areas: Oryol, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Millerovo—in Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; and Hvardiiske—the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
How many were destroyed by air defense
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense had shot down/suppressed 119 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, drones of other types, and three "Banderol"/"Dan-T" drones,
Hits by the enemy’s means of air attack were recorded at 18 locations, as well as the fall of downed targets (debris) at eight locations.
The attack is ongoing; enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: EU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline looms
articles.body:
The EU has agreed to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list, while extending restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals and companies accused of supporting the war on Ukraine for the next three years.
With an end-of-Tuesday deadline looming to preserve the Russia blacklist, the EU’s 27 member states found a compromise that meant delisting the two oligarchs in spite of very few countries wanting this outcome. EU sanctions have to be approved unanimously.
France stunned and infuriated EU governments this month when it called for Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek national, to be removed from the list on “national security” grounds, reported to refer to a prisoner exchange deal involving French nationals and Azerbaijan.
Luxembourg then asked for the same treatment for Fridman, the Russian-Israeli magnate, who is suing the Grand Duchy for $16bn (£12bn) for freezing his assets.
The exemptions angered many EU countries which believe it sets a bad precedent by allowing member states to weaken sanctions in defence of national interests.
Ukraine criticised the removal of the men from the sanctions list as unacceptable. Shortly after the decision emerged, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on social media: “No name on the sanctions list is there by accident: each one represents a reason why this war started and continues to this day.”
The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called the decision “shameful and unjustifiable” on X. “Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he added.
In order to enable the delistings that many EU member states found unpalatable, it was proposed that the sanctions be rolled over for 36 months, rather than the usual six.
A spokesperson for Ireland’s EU presidency, which brokered the talks, said the bloc had reached “a difficult compromise”. They said: “Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.”
A decision had been expected earlier this week, but Latvia’s government, facing parliamentary elections on 3 October, announced a last-minute objection to the delistings on Monday. Latvia’s prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, said late on Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise and instructed his foreign minister to enter talks with Paris and Brussels to find a solution.
Diplomats said Latvia had finally agreed to abstain on the two delistings. The blacklist includes Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, as well as Duma deputies, the country’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex.
Senior EU officials have promised to present about 1,600 new designations – individuals and entities involved in the Russian military industrial complex – to foreign ministers next month. But the latest standoff, which followed the tortuous agreement on the EU’s 21st round of sanctions in July, suggests the process could be difficult.

articles.title: Celebrities at the Pentagon: How unusual was the Paul brothers’ visit?
articles.body:
Celebrities at the Pentagon: How unusual was the Paul brothers’ visit?
Logan and Jake Paul face social media backlash after Pentagon visit with Pete Hegseth.
Influencers Logan and Jake Paul are the latest celebrities to visit the Pentagon, where they addressed troops and met with United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The Paul brothers, who made the visit on Thursday, are content creators and are also known for combat sports. They shared photos and videos of the visit over the weekend on social media. The posts also included images from a separate meeting with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Could US pull one-third of troops from Europe? What that would mean
- list 2 of 4Trump says US has ‘permanent control’ of Greenland security: Does it?
- list 3 of 4Influencers Jake and Logan Paul visit the Pentagon
- list 4 of 4US strikes on alleged drug boats may be ‘crimes against humanity’, UN says
It remains unclear why the two visited the Pentagon, but the appearance comes amid a broader push to promote martial arts and physical fitness among service members, including efforts to recruit troops to attend the UFC event held at the White House in June.
The visit also comes ahead of the “State of the Force” address, Hegseth’s annual speech to troops slated for later this month. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Hegseth asked commanders to nominate troops to attend the address, where they could also have the opportunity to “work out” with him.
Is it unusual for a celebrity to visit the Pentagon?
Celebrities and other public figures have visited the Pentagon during multiple administrations.
In 2019, during US President Donald Trump’s first term in office, actor Milo Ventimiglia of the television show This Is Us visited the Pentagon to discuss ways to strengthen the “civilian-military connection”. In 2018, actor Gerard Butler also visited the Pentagon to discuss his film Hunter Killer, which was made in collaboration with the US Navy.
Gene Simmons, the frontman of the band KISS and a prominent supporter of the military and veterans, visited the Pentagon in 2019 and addressed service members and reporters in the press room.
Such visits also took place during the administration of former US President Joe Biden, a Democrat. Actor David Boreanaz toured the Pentagon in October 2024 as part of a United Service Organizations (USO) tour, in which celebrities, musicians and other public figures travel to military bases around the world to entertain US service members. Boreanaz was there in connection with his role in the television series SEAL Team.
During the administration of former US President Barack Obama, the Pentagon also shared information with filmmakers Mark Boal and Kathryn Bigelow on the hunt for Osama bin Laden, details that they used in the making of Zero Dark Thirty, a film about the operation that led to bin Laden’s killing. The visit was controversial because it gave the filmmakers unusually extensive access to the Pentagon’s workings.
Are the Paul brothers particularly controversial?
The Paul brothers have been embroiled in controversy for years. Last week, Jake Paul said the Second Amendment of the US Constitution, which protects the right to bear arms, needs “updating”, claiming that shotguns and pistols would not be able to “upthrow” the government if needed, as weapon systems become more advanced.
“We maybe need to be able to bear more advanced weapons systems as citizens,” Paul told an influencer at the All-In Summit.
In 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) charged Jake Paul over his promotion of Tronix (TRX), a cryptocurrency created by crypto entrepreneur Justin Sun. The SEC said he failed to disclose that he was paid about $25,000 in cryptocurrency to promote it in 2021 on X, then known as Twitter.
The brothers built their fame in part through stunts designed to attract attention. Logan Paul, for example, posted a video on YouTube that showed the body of an apparent suicide victim in Japan’s Aokigahara forest, colloquially dubbed the “suicide forest”, and made jokes at the victim’s expense before eventually removing the video.
Jake Paul was charged with trespassing after he was filmed inside an Arizona shopping mall during unrest and looting amid nationwide Black Lives Matter protests over the killing of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer in May 2020. The charges against Jake Paul were later dropped.
What has the reaction been to the visit?
The visit prompted backlash. Adam Kinzinger, a former Republican congressman, reposted a video of the visit, writing, “We aren’t a serious country at the moment.”
Progressive media outlet MeidasTouch Network also criticised the visit, writing, “Idiocracy didn’t go far enough,” in response to the clip.
The comments were among widespread criticism on social media in response to the brothers’ visit.
In a lengthy post of his own, Jake Paul pushed back against the criticism.
“Because I’d rather be in the room asking questions, learning, challenging ideas, building relationships, and figuring out how I can help than sitting behind a screen telling everyone else what they should be doing,” Jake Paul said.

articles.title: Tsikhanouskaya warns Russia could use Belarus for new attacks on Ukraine
articles.body:
Exiled Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said the threat of Russia using Belarusian territory to launch new attacks against Ukraine is "a real possibility," as reported by Ukrinform on Sept. 23.
"If Russia at some point again wants to attack Ukraine in any way from the northern border, then (Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko) will be very happy to provide territory, logistics, and Belarusian infrastructure to help Putin achieve his goals," Tsikhanouskaya told Ukrinform on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has increasingly warned that Russia might open a new front against northern Ukraine and attempt to draw Belarus deeper into the war.
Lukashenko, who allowed Russian forces to use Belarusian territory as a staging ground for the 2022 Kyiv offensive, denied such plans on May 21 and proposed a meeting with Zelensky in either Belarus or Ukraine.
Tsikhanouskaya said Belarusian infrastructure is already being used to support Russian drone operations, including logistics and equipment for directing drones.
The comments come after Ukrainian officials said on Sept. 14 that Russia is using Belarusian infrastructure, including LTE networks and repeater stations, to help maintain stable signals for Shahed-type drones during attacks on Ukraine.
Tsikhanouskaya also said repeaters were being installed along Belarus' borders with Ukraine and EU countries, which she warned could facilitate future Russian attacks or provocations.
She added that Lukashenko has benefited economically from Russia's war, claiming that more than 500 Belarusian companies produce components, including optics and microchips, for the Russian military, supply petroleum products to Russia, and help Moscow circumvent sanctions.
Tsikhanouskaya also pointed to Belarus' cooperation with Russian online retailer Wildberries, saying the Belarusian regime was developing warehouses for the company.
Wildberries has become a target of Ukraine's long-range drone campaign in recent months. Ukrainian forces struck at least several of the company's logistics facilities across Russia in July and August. Zelensky said some of the targeted warehouses were being used to supply the Russian military, including with navigation equipment and components for drone production.
Tsikhanouskaya said Lukashenko would like Russia to win the war because Moscow is his main political and economic ally. She argued that a weakened Russian President Vladimir Putin would mean less support for the Belarusian regime.
Belarus held military exercises near its borders with Poland and Lithuania from Sept. 15 to 18, the Belarusian Defense Ministry said on Sept. 15.
The Belarusian Defense Ministry described the drills as "defensive" and said they are aimed at improving the military's ability to "protect the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity."
Belarus is also building new railway infrastructure in the country's southern Gomel Oblast that will be capable of receiving military trains carrying personnel and heavy equipment, the Belarusian Railway Workers' Community reported on Aug. 24.

articles.title: Trump’s U.N. Address Offers a Doctrine of Peace Through Force
articles.body:
In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, President Donald Trump spun a familiar web of rhetoric regarding U.S. foreign policy—one that highlights force as a method of achieving peace.
In a speech that moved from Iran to Venezuela, Cuba, and beyond, Trump presented something approaching a foreign-policy doctrine: American military might is not the alternative to diplomacy but the leverage that makes it possible.
David Satterfield, Director of Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy, tells TIME that the speech Tuesday demonstrates a position held by the Trump Administration that “force is the only currency of value.”
“The strong do as they will and the weak suffer as they must,” he says, further characterizing the approach.
In Trump’s telling, strength is not merely a deterrent. It is something to be used—through military action and economic isolation—to force negotiations or impose an outcome.
How Trump defines ‘peace through strength’
Trump has repeatedly distilled his foreign policy strategy into three words: “peace through strength.” The examples he gave of this policy in action illustrate how he may see the U.S. functioning as a global enforcer going forward.
His definition of the phrase has previously been suggested by its use in Department of Defense ads and in his online endorsements of fellow Republicans. He recently credited this approach for the joint U.S.-Israel strikes that initiated the current conflict with Iran, posting to Truth Social in March: “PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH TO PUT IT MILDLY!!!”
Trump’s approach also encompasses economic coercion. In the case of Iran, he said the U.S. had initially offered economic cooperation, turned to military action when Tehran refused, and was now seeking its “complete economic isolation” to push it back toward negotiations.
Trump grouped Cuba among those affected by U.S. economic pressure campaigns on Tuesday. He described a government under mounting strain and predicted political change, declaring that Cuba was a “failed” nation but that “freedom will be coming.” Cuban delegates departed in protest.
Yet Trump presented such coercion as compatible with his role as a global peacemaker. He claimed credit for resolving eight wars since returning to office, although that claim has been widely disputed.
In tandem, these elements suggest that Trump sees taking action as a superior means of enacting change. He proposes the approaches as being almost diametrically opposed: While others only speak of making a difference, he acts.
“While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them,” Trump said in front of the General Assembly. “While others have talked of courage, America has shown it.”
Satterfield says that this speech is mostly “old wine rebottled” for Trump. But it clarified how the President is applying his longstanding ideas today: using military action and economic coercion not merely to deter adversaries, but to force negotiations and shape political outcomes.
Trump defends military force against Iran and drug cartels
While Trump sees Iran as an example of his “peace through strength” ethos, the conflict is ongoing, and it remains to be seen how it fits into the pattern that he is hoping to establish.
Addressing the topic seemed all but unavoidable heading into the General Assembly. In doing so, Trump said that he had a choice ahead of him: Move forward with a peace deal or “annihilate the Islamic Republic.”
The comments came amid stalled negotiations in the war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
Members of Iran’s delegation walked out during Trump’s remarks, an immediate demonstration of the gulf between his coercive message and the adversary that he may hope to persuade by it.
In his speech, he also issued threats against cartel leaders, defending his campaign of drone strikes against suspected drug boats in the Caribbean. These strikes have been criticized by international organizations, legal experts, and human rights groups, which state that the military actions violate international law and constitute extrajudicial killings.
“The cartels are the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere—not good people,” he said. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled, or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing.”
But while these messages are largely meant to promote the very strength that Trump relies upon in his endeavors, the potency of his remarks may be dwindling amid contested claims of success.
Venezuela is Trump’s ‘peace through strength’ model. But Iran is testing its limits
Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, a fellow for the Middle East at the Baker Institute, tells TIME that Trump’s speech seems “consistent with the narrative of American dominance” that he has long used to justify military action.
Trump suggested Tuesday that he considers Venezuela a leading example. In January, the U.S. military launched Operation Absolute Resolve—a nighttime raid in Caracas that captured Venezuela’s president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. Both were transported to New York City to face federal drug-trafficking indictments.
The move paved the way for a transition of power in Venezuela, with former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez ascending to the role of acting President. It also led to an August agreement giving a U.S.-linked venture a controlling stake and long-term development rights in fields containing an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil. Trump said the deal “more than doubles” American oil reserves.
“We’re working closely with the leaders of Venezuela to forge a much better future for the Venezuelan people,” Trump said in his speech. “Last month we signed the largest oil deal in history, covering 65 billion barrels of oil, which will benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously.”
Trump also suggested that U.S. actions had established peace and a route to prosperity for Venezuelans. However, with an acting President who is yet to be elected making deals that may take years to reach fruition, and are likely to draw legal challenges in the meantime, the full picture remains to be seen.
But there is one thing the Venezuela operation might have helped accomplish, which is to establish a potential pattern of a U.S. foreign policy that is defined by unilateral intervention. Following a large show of force, Trump has been quick to claim victory, even while the impact of U.S. involvement is still playing out for the people whom it directly affects.
Another example is the conflict between Israel and Hamas. In his remarks, Trump gave himself credit for ending the war in Gaza, even though key aspects of the peace deal Trump helped broker in October 2025—including Hamas’s disarmament, a long-term governance plan, and the delivery of needed humanitarian aid in Gaza—are largely stalled.
Perceived success in Venezuela “arguably triggered the overreach that we saw in the decision to begin military operations against Iran without a Plan B if initial objectives were not achieved,” Ulrichsen says.
But the limitations of such rhetoric are most “visible” in the Iran conflict, according to Ulrichsen, who says the U.S. has not been able to “translate rhetoric into gains on the ground.”
Trump has repeatedly predicted that the war would end after the November midterm elections, saying last week that it would end “immediately after” them. He endorsed this belief on Tuesday, as well. Trump initially told reporters that U.S. envoys had held a “very good” three-hour meeting with “mediators of Iran."
“They had a very good meeting, and we'll see how it turns out. But certainly, it's to their advantage to make a deal, and we can do that,” he said.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior nonresident fellow at the Center for International Policy, emphasized the point that concrete outcomes in the Middle East may prove critical for Trump.
“President Trump’s ‘peace through strength’ approach has yet to produce the agreement he wants with Iran,” Mortazavi says. “Trump’s argument leaves a central question unanswered: How does further destruction secure an agreement on Washington’s terms when the pressure so far has not?”
“For now, Trump can point to the damage U.S. forces have inflicted, but the war’s central political disputes remain unresolved,” she adds.
The outcomes of these most recent efforts—and whether they moved the needle on peace efforts—remain undetermined. Subsequently, Trump turned to the same takeaway that he shared in his speech, which is that Iran is facing either “potential greatness or obliteration.”
“It does seem as if such rhetoric is producing diminishing results as his tone gradually loses its shock value,” Ulrichsen observes.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: We are ready not to strike Russian energy facilities if they do not strike ours
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: We are ready not to strike Russian energy facilities if they do not strike ours
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US will convey Ukraine's proposal for an energy truce to Russia.
Source: Zelenskyy's press conference after his meeting with US President Donald Trump on 22 September
Quote: "We are ready. I'm not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire. We are ready for an energy ceasefire if they do not attack our energy system, our electricity, heating, and water supply.
This is our proposal. We are thankful to the American side. They will share it with the Russians. I don't know the Russian position."
Details: Zelenskyy added that he is grateful to the US side for conveying this proposal to Russia.
He also expressed hope that the US will find a way to bring Russia and Ukraine to negotiations.
He said he had discussed the winter with his US counterpart Donald Trump, including a package of missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
According to Zelenskyy, nobody said no when asked about supplying Ukraine with the missiles, but there was no specific answer.
Zelenskyy also said that Trump had not asked Ukraine to unilaterally stop strikes on Russia. Instead, they had discussed an energy truce.
Zelenskyy believes Putin will tell everyone that he is ready to end the war before the elections. However, he said that after the elections, there will be attacks, with Putin then claiming that they had been carried out because of Ukraine.
Zelenskyy added that there had been an attack the previous night and that Ukrainian intelligence already knew that the Russians were saying it had supposedly been carried out because Ukraine had attacked during the elections.
Background: Before the conversation, US President Donald Trump said he would discuss with Zelenskyy the possibility of granting Ukraine licences to produce missiles for Patriot systems.

articles.title: Latvia to impose national sanctions on Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman after EU compromise
articles.body:
Latvia to impose national sanctions on Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman after EU compromise
Latvia will impose national sanctions on the Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman after making concessions and lifting its veto on their removal from the EU sanctions list.
Source: European Pravda, citing a statement by the Latvian government on 22 September
Details: Latvia's Cabinet of Ministers has instructed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to immediately draw up a proposal, legal justification and the necessary draft legislation to enable Latvia to impose national sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman.
Quote: "Latvia will continue to use all legal instruments at its disposal to prevent the unfreezing of these individuals' funds and economic resources in Latvia."
More details: The Cabinet of Ministers also said that at a closed meeting on 22 September, it had agreed on Latvia's position on extending EU sanctions against Russia. The deal ensured that personal sanctions against more than 2,600 Russian supporters of the war and related individuals and entities would be extended for the next three years. Up until now, the decision has had to be taken every six months.
During the procedure for the adoption of the decision by the Council of the EU, however, Latvia's representative will abstain from voting in order to maintain and publicly express Latvia's political opposition to the lifting of EU sanctions on the two oligarchs.
"Throughout the negotiations with the leaders of EU member states, Latvia opposed the removal of politically motivated individuals from the individual sanctions list and was the only EU member state to maintain this position until the very end. It was the morally right position, and our allies in Ukraine appreciated it," Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said.
He added that "this was not a choice between a good and a bad decision, but between a bad one and a much worse one – a choice between changing the status of two individuals and the future of the entire sanctions regime".
Quote from Kulbergs: "By deciding to continue imposing sanctions on these individuals, we have achieved an outcome that is more beneficial for Latvia, Ukraine and Europe in the long term."
Background:
- Amid the announcement of Riga's decision, it was reported that French President Emmanuel Macron has agreed to begin talks with Latvia on joining France's nuclear deterrence initiative, and that France has committed to strengthening its military presence in Latvia.
- European Pravda sources in French diplomatic circles explained why Paris wanted to lift sanctions on Usmanov. It later emerged that France planned to "exchange" Usmanov's delisting for the release of several French citizens who are currently in prison in Azerbaijan.

articles.title: Netanyahu to cut short NYC trip amid protests, Mamdani threat
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Netanyahu to cut short NYC visit amid protests, Mamdani arrest threat
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has dramatically shortened his visit to New York for the UN General Assembly, amid planned protests, heightened security and tensions with Mayor Zohran Mamdani over the International Criminal Court warrant for his arrest.
Netanyahu is expected to arrive in the US on Thursday morning, address the General Assembly at 2pm New York time and leave for Israel later that evening, according to Israeli media reports.
The Israeli leader is not expected to spend a single night in the US, cutting what had initially been planned as a longer visit to just several hours. He has also cancelled a planned stop in Texas to meet billionaire Elon Musk and will not take Israeli journalists aboard his official "Wing of Zion" aircraft.
Israeli media cited planned protests and security concerns among the reasons for the unusually brief visit.
According to Ynet, Netanyahu's plane is expected to avoid New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport and instead land in neighbouring New Jersey.
The outlet linked the arrangements partly to tensions with Mamdani, who has repeatedly called for Netanyahu to face arrest over the ICC warrant.
Other Israeli reporting, however, has attributed the decision to avoid JFK to logistical and security considerations surrounding Netanyahu's aircraft.
Mamdani has been an outspoken critic of Netanyahu and previously pledged to have the Israeli leader arrested if he travelled to New York, citing the ICC warrant issued against him in November 2024.
The mayor acknowledged in July, however, that New York City does not independently possess the legal authority to enforce the warrant.
"It is clear that we do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant," Mamdani said at the time, while calling on the US federal government to join the ICC and execute it.
He has nevertheless maintained that Netanyahu is not welcome in New York and has continued to describe him as a war criminal over Israel's actions in Gaza.
The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli defence minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024, saying there were reasonable grounds to believe they bore criminal responsibility for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Israel's war on Gaza.
Israel rejects the allegations and does not recognise the court's jurisdiction. The US is also not a member of the ICC.
US President Donald Trump said in July that Netanyahu would not be arrested in the United States.
Heavy security and protests expected
Netanyahu is expected to receive unusually heavy security protection during his brief stay, with US Secret Service involvement in preparations for the visit reportedly greater than usual.
Large demonstrations are also expected in New York during his visit.
Haaretz reported that Netanyahu is preparing for a hostile reception both on the streets and inside the General Assembly, where Israeli officials anticipate that ambassadors and other delegates could walk out or stage protests during his speech.
A mass walkout took place when Netanyahu addressed the General Assembly last year.
Mamdani has said he does not plan to participate in protests against Netanyahu during the visit and has been coordinating with the New York Police Department over security surrounding UNGA.
Netanyahu is not expected to meet Trump during the trip, and a meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also not been confirmed.
His address comes around a month before Israel's general election, with Israeli media reporting that the speech is expected to focus heavily on Iran while also being aimed at a domestic Israeli audience.
Israeli officials are meanwhile hoping protests inside the General Assembly will be smaller than last year, amid international attention on the war with Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Israel continues to occupy most of the Gaza Strip and carry out deadly air strikes, shelling and gunfire despite the October 2025 ceasefire.
More than 73,900 Palestinians have been killed and nearly 175,000 wounded since October 2023, including around 1,400 killed since the ceasefire took effect.
Most of Gaza's roughly 2.1 million people remain displaced, while Israeli restrictions continue to impede the entry of critical humanitarian and reconstruction supplies.

articles.title: Poland Deploys Military Aviation as Russia Strikes Ukraine, Rzeszów and Lublin Airports Suspend Flights
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Poland Deploys Military Aviation as Russia Strikes Ukraine, Rzeszów and Lublin Airports Suspend Flights
Poland deployed military aircraft, air defense systems, and electronic reconnaissance assets on September 23 in response to renewed Russian strikes on Ukraine, while airports in Rzeszów and Lublin temporarily suspended operations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command said military aviation had begun operating in Polish airspace as Russia carried out attacks against Ukraine using airborne weapons.
“In connection with the strikes by the Russian Federation on the territory of Ukraine, carried out using airborne assault means, military aviation operations have commenced in Polish airspace,” the command said.
Polish authorities also activated the necessary air defense and equipment to protect the country’s airspace during the Russian attack.
The heightened military activity also affected civilian aviation. The Polish Air Navigation Services Agency reported that airports in Rzeszów and Lublin temporarily suspended operations to ensure military aircraft had sufficient freedom to operate.
Later, both airports resumed normal operations after the Polish military operation concluded.
The September 23 deployment follows a similar response less than a week earlier. On September 17, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Russian drone strikes had taken place in Ukraine’s Volyn region near the Polish border.
Poland scrambled military aircraft in response, while operations at the same airports in Lublin and Rzeszów were temporarily suspended.
The latest Polish response came as Russia launched another drone attack on Ukraine, including Kyiv. The September 23 strike on the Ukrainian capital killed at least one person and injured seven others, with strikes and falling debris reported across several districts, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Klitschko said one of the victims, who had been hospitalized in serious condition, later died from their injuries. Four other people remained hospitalized following the attack.

articles.title: Foreign volunteers retrain as drone operators as Ukraine’s battlefield changes
articles.body:
Four foreign volunteers serving in the Babai rifle battalion are training to operate FPV drones in Ternopil Oblast in western Ukraine, where they have formed a dedicated drone team, Suspilne reported on 22 September.
Ukraine's military increasingly looks to unmanned systems for roles traditionally carried out by soldiers. In May, an adviser to the commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps said the corps planned to replace roughly 30% of its infantry with ground robotic systems by the end of 2026 "to save the lives of our soldiers." The plan concerns ground robots rather than FPV aircraft, but reflects the broader move toward using unmanned systems on the battlefield.
From mortars to FPV drones
The team was assembled by Harry, a British volunteer who has fought in Ukraine since arriving in March 2022. He served as a machine gunner in Kharkiv and during the Kharkiv counter-offensive, as well as in Bakhmut and Zaporizhzhia.
Before coming to Ukraine, Harry served with People's Defense forces against ISIS in Syria. He said Ukraine's battlefield is fundamentally different, with drones and artillery making combat more dangerous.
For Fuzzy, a former British Army infantryman and counterterrorism specialist, the transition came after more than two years as a mortar operator. He arrived in April 2022 and initially trained Ukrainian defenders before moving into combat roles.
Fuzzy said he had initially been reluctant to switch from mortars to FPVs but found the drones not as difficult to operate as he had expected after training for more than two months.
Not everyone on the team flies. Rupert, who served in the British and Israeli armies, called Ukraine the clearest case of right against wrong since 1939 and said anyone who does nothing will regret it. His role on the team is technical: setting up antennas and checking drones before flights. "The younger guys can fly," he said.
Mac, an American with no previous military service, joined the war in a different role. He arrived in February 2025 and served with the Azov brigade as a logistics specialist in Donbas. Ukraine first appeared on his radar with the 2014 Maidan protests, he said, and when Russia's full-scale invasion began—"seeing the massacre in Bucha, the maternity hospital blown up in Mariupol"—he called it a higher calling and began preparing to come.
Adapting to the battlefield
The volunteers came to Ukraine with different backgrounds and have taken different roles during the war. Harry assembled the FPV team from fighters he had served with in different Ukrainian units. Fuzzy said the changing nature of the war made the transition necessary.
"The war has changed so much that what I was teaching could no longer be applied everywhere," Fuzzy added. "At this stage of the war, we have to keep pace with the times—everything is improving now."
Harry said his long-term goal is to live permanently in Ukraine and open a business. "I see Ukraine as my home," he said. "I want to defend not just the Ukrainian people but also the place where I want to live the rest of my life."
